name: The Network That Tried to Harness the Eyes to Harvest the World

c8a65c9d1e89adf9.h:
Biological Constant — Pre-History to Present

Human Visual Perception

Pre-Condition (Human Vulnerability) · period on the page's diagram: 400 BCE – 1620 CE · Ancient & Medieval Roots

Before any philosopher acted, the visual system already delivered the isolated self: a single point of view behind the eyes, looking out at a world of separate objects

What they did

Close one eye, then open it. Look at your hand, then at the wall behind it. Notice what the experience feels like: you are behind your eyes, looking out at things that are separate from you. Your hand is one object. The wall is another. You are the observer. The world is what you observe.

This is perspectival vision — binocular sight organized from a single spatial locus and directed outward. It produces a structure that can be read as confirming a subject–object universe: I am in here, the world is out there, and the world is made of distinct bounded things. That reading feels so natural that it barely registers as an interpretation at all. It feels like what seeing simply is.

Why — the gain and control

This is precisely what made perspectival vision useful to the deliberate actors in this network. A philosophy that defines you as a bounded observer of an external object-world becomes much easier to install when your eyes appear to confirm it every time you open them. The framework seems to rest on immediate sensory evidence rather than institutional authority. The actors did not have to build the isolated self from scratch — they had a perceptual experience they could point to and say: see, you already know this is true.

The same perceptual architecture supports radically different philosophical conclusions — every indigenous and non-dualist tradition looked through the same eyes and arrived somewhere else entirely. So the affordance alone produced nothing. It required institutional pressure to select one interpretation, promote it, and hold it in place.

Maurice Merleau-Ponty (Phenomenology of Perception, 1945) showed that raw perceptual experience is fundamentally more entangled than the subject–object framework allows — that Western philosophy imposed the split onto perception rather than discovering it there. The ease with which the imposition succeeded, however, owes something to the spatial structure of vision itself.

Thomas Nagel (The View from Nowhere, 1986) analyzed how the philosophical aspiration toward objectivity draws rhetorical force from the directional structure of sight, even though vision itself does not require or produce that aspiration.

Primary sources
  • Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985): documented how the Royal Society's experimental practice encoded specific authority relationships inherited from Church institutional culture.
  • Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972): traced the esoteric and commercial networks that preceded the Royal Society's formation.
All connections

Descartes (convergence), Newton (convergence), Royal Society (convergence)

4848dc0a9533108f.h:
Europe, ~1500–1800

European Merchant & Colonial Capital

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Funded the philosophy that made the world look like a set of ownable, exploitable objects

What they did

The merchant and colonial trading class — the East India Companies, the Dutch and British trading empires, the banking families of Amsterdam, Venice, and London — were primary funders of early modern natural philosophy. They sponsored voyages that collected natural specimens, funded the instruments the new science required, and sat on the boards of the Royal Society. The Encyclopédie's network ran through Swiss commercial publishers. Darwin's Beagle voyage served British imperial and commercial interests directly.

Why — the gain and control

A philosophy that treats the world as inert matter — with no inherent sacred relationships, no spiritual ownership — is a philosophy that makes the world a free resource for whoever has capital to extract it. Land without inherent sanctity can be taken. Animals without inherent value can be farmed to exhaustion. The merchant class funded knowledge that made the world look like what they needed it to be: ownable, measurable, extractable. This was not incidental to the content of early modern science. It shaped it.

Primary sources
  • Robert Darnton, The Business of Enlightenment (1979): documented how the Encyclopédie's commercial production inseparably linked ideas and market interest.
  • Joyce Appleby, Economic Thought and Ideology in Seventeenth-Century England (1978): traced the relationship between commercial interests and the new natural philosophy.
All connections

Royal Society (documented), The Encyclopédie (documented), Charles Darwin (inferred)

6a893c2a7a67e904.h:
Britain, ~1660–1960

British Imperial State & Crown

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

Chartered the institutions, employed the philosophers, and deployed a global education system

What they did

The British Crown chartered the Royal Society in 1660 — an official stamp of legitimacy on the new mechanical philosophy. The East India Company, a Crown-chartered monopoly, employed James and John Stuart Mill, who produced the philosophical justifications for colonial dispossession while sitting at company desks. The Crown funded British Museum collections that provided the material base for Darwin and Huxley. The Colonial Office deployed an education system that replaced indigenous knowledge globally. These were not incidental relationships — the state was the administrative backbone of the network.

Why — the gain and control

An empire cannot sustainably govern a quarter of the world through force alone. The most efficient long-term control is a population that understands reality through your categories, values achievement on your terms, and has been separated from knowledge systems that told them they belonged to the land. The education investment was colonial infrastructure — cheaper per capita than armies and more durable than garrisons. Macaulay did not frame his 1835 Minute as ontological engineering; he framed it as administrative efficiency and the self-evident superiority of Western civilization. The destruction of indigenous knowledge systems was described as clearing away superstition, not suppressing alternative metaphysics. The ontological effect — populations understanding themselves through categories presupposing individual property rights, secular rationality, and the illegitimacy of communal land tenure — was documented by scholars (Frantz Fanon, Ngugi wa Thiong'o, Ranajit Guha) but was not the architects' stated purpose.

Primary sources
  • Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind (1986): primary account of how British colonial education dismantled African ways of knowing.
  • Gauri Viswanathan, Masks of Conquest (1989): documented how English literary education functioned as ideological apparatus in British India.
All connections

British Empire Education System (documented), T.H. Huxley + The X Club (inferred)

212e45d0ab2a2cb4.h:
USA, ~1870–1930

American Industrial Capital Class

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Carnegie, Rockefeller — funded the philosophy that made their monopolies look like the law of nature

What they did

Carnegie and Rockefeller, along with Vanderbilt, Morgan, Frick, and dozens of others who together controlled the American economy in the Gilded Age, paid for Herbert Spencer's American lecture tours, distributed his books, and used his "survival of the fittest" framework in public speeches while running coordinated cartels in private. Rockefeller funded the founding of the University of Chicago in 1890 — which became the institution that produced the economists who would run global economic governance in the second half of the 20th century.

Why — the gain and control

The investment was explicit: fund the ideas that make your practices look like natural law, and place those ideas in the institution that trains the people who will govern. Carnegie ran monopolies while publicly citing open-market competition as cosmic truth. Rockefeller's private letters show a man who ran an engineered industrial system while publicly framing it as natural selection. The return on a single founding gift, measured in regulatory immunity across generations, was the highest-ROI investment either man ever made.

Primary sources
  • Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944): documented the American reception of Spencer's ideas and the industrial funding behind it.
  • Ron Chernow, Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller Sr. (1998): documented the relationship between Rockefeller's private strategy and his public philosophical commitments.
All connections

Carnegie & Rockefeller Network (documented), Herbert Spencer (documented), Chicago School of Economics (inferred)

USA, ~1870–1930

American Industrial Capital Class

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Carnegie, Rockefeller — funded the philosophy that made their monopolies look like the law of nature

What they did

Carnegie and Rockefeller, along with Vanderbilt, Morgan, Frick, and dozens of others who together controlled the American economy in the Gilded Age, paid for Herbert Spencer's American lecture tours, distributed his books, and used his "survival of the fittest" framework in public speeches while running coordinated cartels in private. Rockefeller funded the founding of the University of Chicago in 1890 — which became the institution that produced the economists who would run global economic governance in the second half of the 20th century.

Why — the gain and control

The investment was explicit: fund the ideas that make your practices look like natural law, and place those ideas in the institution that trains the people who will govern. Carnegie ran monopolies while publicly citing open-market competition as cosmic truth. Rockefeller's private letters show a man who ran an engineered industrial system while publicly framing it as natural selection. The return on a single founding gift, measured in regulatory immunity across generations, was the highest-ROI investment either man ever made.

Primary sources
  • Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944): documented the American reception of Spencer's ideas and the industrial funding behind it.
  • Ron Chernow, Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller Sr. (1998): documented the relationship between Rockefeller's private strategy and his public philosophical commitments.

bf89f79ec94cbbe2.h:
USA, ~1947–1985

US Cold War National Security State

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Secretly funded Western liberal academics and exported their worldview as counter-programming to Soviet ideology

What they did

The CIA ran the Congress for Cultural Freedom (CCF), which secretly funded Western arts journals, academic conferences, and intellectual publications as counter-programming to Soviet cultural influence. The stated goals were political: demonstrate the vitality of Western liberal culture, attract non-aligned intellectuals away from communist affiliation, and discredit Soviet claims that Western democracy suppressed dissent. There is no archival evidence of a parallel goal to spread materialist secular individualism as a coordinated metaphysical program. What the CCF promoted — pluralism, liberal democracy, individual artistic freedom, anti-dogmatism — carried an implicit philosophical framework, but that framework was its unexamined premise, not its agenda. The Ford Foundation — closely tied to US foreign policy apparatus — funded training that sent Chilean economists to the University of Chicago, producing the "Chicago Boys" who implemented the neoliberal framework under Pinochet. The Defense Department shaped academic research priorities across American universities, channeling funding toward fields serving Cold War goals.

Why — the gain and control

The US national security establishment understood by the 1950s that the Cold War was a contest over which framework populations would use to understand reality. Funding the academic infrastructure spreading liberal secular individualism — the view that free individuals in free markets are the natural order — was foreign policy. It was less expensive than armies and more durable than coups. The worldview it funded aligned with American capital's economic interests, creating a self-reinforcing system: what was strategically useful was also what funders believed was true.

Primary sources
  • Frances Stonor Saunders, The Cultural Cold War (1999): documented the CIA's Congress for Cultural Freedom and its secret funding of Western intellectual life.
  • George Reisch, How the Cold War Transformed Philosophy of Science (2005): documented how Cold War politics shaped the spread of logical positivism in American universities.

789713d607c7ae4e.h:
~1947–present

Postwar Corporate & Finance Network

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

Koch, Scaife, Volker Fund — a coordinated long game that institutionalized the metaphysical claim that humans are naturally self-interested, that greed is virtue, that power is moral authority, and that the market is the measure of all worth

What they did

The Mont Pelerin Society (1947), the Volker Fund, Richard Mellon Scaife, the Olin Foundation, the Bradley Foundation, and the Koch brothers built a coordinated pipeline: fund the metaphysical assumptions in the academy, then translate them into law schools, economics departments, business schools, and eventually policy. The output was not just regulatory capture — it was a specific picture of what human beings fundamentally are.

The doctrine disseminated through this network held that self-interest is the only genuine virtue and altruism a form of moral corruption or self-deception. Milton Friedman's 1970 New York Times essay stated the position explicitly: "the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits" — the rest is theft from shareholders. Friedrich Hayek argued that any collective moral goal beyond individual exchange was the road to totalitarianism. Ayn Rand, whose work was actively distributed and promoted by this network, made the metaphysical claim structurally explicit: the individual sovereign self in a meaningless universe is the only real unit of value; altruism is not noble self-sacrifice but the sacrifice of the real (the individual) to the unreal (the collective).

The Nietzschean strand was systematically distorted by this network. Nietzsche's will to power — originally a critique of herd morality and a call for self-overcoming — was skewed into a justification for dominance hierarchies: the powerful are powerful because they are better. Combined with Spencer's Social Darwinism (which Darwin himself rejected as misapplication), the network disseminated a unified metaphysical package: the universe is an empty competitive arena, humans are natural competitors, the wealthy and powerful are the fittest, poverty is selection in action, and intervention on behalf of the weak is a violation of natural law.

This was not organic intellectual development. It was a coordinated long game with documented funding and documented intent. The Olin Foundation explicitly funded law-and-economics programs at Harvard, Chicago, and Yale to insert market-as-moral-arbiter assumptions into legal reasoning. The Koch network's internal strategy documents — released through litigation — describe academic and political funding as investment mapped against specific regulatory exposures, with measurable returns.

Why — the gain and control

The funders did not typically frame their project as metaphysical engineering. Koch documents describe investment in regulatory outcomes. The Olin Foundation described countering anti-business bias in law schools. The Volker Fund described defending economic freedom. What they funded was a complete philosophical apparatus — Friedman, Hayek, Rand, Buchanan — whose combined output was a picture of human nature (self-interested, competitive, material) presented not as ideology but as economic science and natural law. The ontological function — providing a worldview in which extraction appears as natural law — was real regardless of whether the funders recognized it as such. The network funded the ideas that made its practices look like natural law, then placed those ideas inside every institution that trained the professionals who would govern. A person trained in this framework carries the metaphysical assumption not as ideology but as the background definition of what reality is — which is far more powerful than any argument. Ends justified means as a matter of doctrine (the market produces optimal outcomes regardless of how they are reached). Greed was reframed not just as acceptable but as the engine of the good. Power was positioned as its own moral authority. The framing required the complete erasure of any dimension of human experience — relational, ecological, ancestral, spiritual — that could ground an alternative account of value. That erasure was the point.

Primary sources
  • Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits,' New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970: the foundational document of shareholder-primacy doctrine.
  • Friedrich Hayek, The Road to Serfdom (1944): argued that collective moral goals beyond individual exchange are structurally totalitarian.
  • Ayn Rand, The Virtue of Selfishness (1964): the most explicit popular statement that self-interest is the only genuine virtue and altruism is moral corruption.
  • Jane Mayer, Dark Money (2016): documented the Koch network's explicit strategy using internal documents released through litigation.
  • Philip Mirowski, Never Let a Serious Crisis Go to Waste (2013): comprehensive account of the Mont Pelerin / neoliberal network's academic and policy strategy.
  • Nancy MacLean, Democracy in Chains (2017): documented the Olin Foundation's explicit law-and-economics pipeline into Harvard, Chicago, and Yale.

d59495120f046446.h:
London, 1660

Royal Society

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

First institution to officially declare: only what you can measure is real

What they did

Britain's King Charles II chartered this club of gentleman-scientists in 1660. Their formal declaration: only things you can weigh, measure, and predict count as real knowledge — what they called empirical science. Everything that couldn't be measured — spirit, felt meaning, the lived sense of belonging to a living world — was placed outside what serious people discussed. Not refuted. Not argued against. Simply defined out of existence by institutional authority.

Why — the gain and control

The Royal Society was chartered by a Crown that needed a basis for knowledge independent of the Church. But its merchant and commercial members needed a world of measurable, ownable objects. A forest that is spiritually alive has claims on you. A forest that is inert matter measured in board feet does not. The institution served both the state's need for authority over knowledge and the commercial class's need for a philosophy that made nature freely exploitable.

Primary sources
  • Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985): documented the political and social context of the Royal Society's founding.
  • Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972): traced the esoteric and commercial networks that shaped the Royal Society's formation.

b9a2d790f63bd30b.h:
France, 1637–1650

Descartes

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Established: the isolated thinking mind is the only certainty — everything else is inference

What they did

René Descartes stripped away everything — body, senses, world — until only one certainty remained: the fact of his own thinking. Everything else, including the external world, had to be proved from that single interior point. Body became a machine. The world outside became something you deduce, not something you inhabit. This split — self as interior observer versus world as external object — is called mind-body dualism, and it is the philosophical foundation of virtually every subsequent step in this network.

Why — the gain and control

Descartes was trying to establish knowledge independent of Church authority, which was then in crisis. He succeeded — but the framework he found, centered on the isolated individual mind as the only certain point, was immediately useful to every institution that needed people to understand themselves as separate from the world they lived in. You cannot govern, tax, conscript, or sell to a community. You can do all of those things to a collection of isolated individuals.

Primary sources
  • Charles Taylor, Sources of the Self (1989): the most comprehensive account of how Cartesian self-understanding became the foundational structure of Western modernity.
  • Matthew Crawford, The World Beyond Your Head (2015): documented how Cartesian dualism shaped contemporary experience architecture.

a29c5643e599853a.h:
England, 1687

Newton

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Proved the universe is a perfect clockwork — the dominant picture of reality for 200 years

What they did

Newton's Principia showed that planets, tides, and falling objects all obey the same mathematical laws. The universe was a perfect machine — what came to be called the clockwork universe. God wound it up at the start; everything since has been gears turning. If the universe is a machine, bodies are machines. If bodies are machines, people are machines. And in a machine, you are a part that performs a function.

Why — the gain and control

The clockwork universe served the interests of every party that wanted the world to be exploitable. A living world with inherent meaning makes claims on its inhabitants. A machine does not. Newton's image made industrialization, colonization, and mechanized agriculture feel like simply using what was there rather than destroying something that mattered.

Primary sources
  • Richard Westfall, Never at Rest: A Biography of Isaac Newton (1980): the standard scholarly account.
  • Morris Berman, The Reenchantment of the World (1981): traced how Newton's mechanical worldview displaced participatory frameworks.

fe624e78cdfd1c01.h:
England, 1680–1710

John Locke

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Wrote the philosophy of individual rights and private property while invested in the colonial slave trade

What they did

John Locke held shares in the Royal Africa Company, wrote the governing constitution for the Carolina colony, and produced the foundational texts of Western liberal individualism simultaneously. His blank-slate theory of mind said humans have no innate connection to the world — we are empty containers filled by experience alone. His land theory said property belongs to whoever mixes their labor with it — erasing the communal and spiritual relationships to land that every colonized people held.

Why — the gain and control

Locke's philosophy was adopted as the foundation of American democracy and British liberalism because it perfectly served the class writing the constitutions: wealthy men who needed a legal framework that protected private accumulation, justified colonial dispossession, and made the "individual with natural rights" the basic unit — while that individual was, in practice, a propertied white man. The philosophy of liberation was simultaneously the philosophy of enclosure.

Primary sources
  • Barbara Arneil, John Locke and America (1996): documented Locke's role in the colonial enterprise.
  • James Tully, An Approach to Political Philosophy: Locke in Contexts (1993): showed how Locke's property theory justified colonial dispossession.

9314f78bb1370b00.h:
England, 1680–1710

John Locke

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Wrote the philosophy of individual rights and private property while invested in the colonial slave trade

What they did

John Locke held shares in the Royal Africa Company, wrote the governing constitution for the Carolina colony, and produced the foundational texts of Western liberal individualism simultaneously. His blank-slate theory of mind said humans have no innate connection to the world — we are empty containers filled by experience alone. His land theory said property belongs to whoever mixes their labor with it — erasing the communal and spiritual relationships to land that every colonized people held.

Why — the gain and control

Locke's philosophy was adopted as the foundation of American democracy and British liberalism because it perfectly served the class writing the constitutions: wealthy men who needed a legal framework that protected private accumulation, justified colonial dispossession, and made the "individual with natural rights" the basic unit — while that individual was, in practice, a propertied white man. The philosophy of liberation was simultaneously the philosophy of enclosure.

Primary sources
  • Barbara Arneil, John Locke and America (1996): documented Locke's role in the colonial enterprise.
  • James Tully, An Approach to Political Philosophy: Locke in Contexts (1993): showed how Locke's property theory justified colonial dispossession.

6f099a702bfd2fa4.h:
Paris, 1750–1780

Holbach's Salon

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

The most important private dinner network of the 1700s — where humans-as-pure-matter first reached mass readership

What they did

Baron d'Holbach hosted twice-weekly dinners for thirty years. The guest list included Diderot, Helvétius, David Hume, and nearly every leading mind of the French Enlightenment. Holbach published The System of Nature (1770), smuggled as contraband across Europe: matter and motion are all that exists, the soul is a fiction, humans are natural objects governed by physical forces. This view — called philosophical materialism — was the first time someone argued the complete case in popular form.

Why — the gain and control

The French educated middle class embraced this because it struck at two sources of authority simultaneously: the Church (which claimed a monopoly on the soul) and the aristocracy (which claimed divine right to rule). The ideas were genuinely liberating in that direction. But the same framework — humans as physical beings in a physical world governed by natural forces — was immediately available for the next set of power-holders to use.

Primary sources
  • Jonathan Israel, Radical Enlightenment (2001): placed Holbach's circle at the center of the materialist philosophical revolution.
  • Alan Kors, D'Holbach's Coterie (1976): the primary scholarly account of the salon's membership and influence.
All connections

David Hume (documented), The Encyclopédie (documented), La Mettrie & Mechanistic Materialism (documented), Democritus, Epicurus & Lucretius (inferred), Royal Society (inferred), Büchner & Scientific Materialists (inferred), French Revolution & Dechristianization (inferred), Newton (inferred)

f53fef0d3ef1096d.h:
Paris, 1751–1772

The Encyclopédie

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

First attempt to reorganize all human knowledge around physical science and reason — with God removed

What they did

Diderot and d'Alembert's 28-volume Encyclopédie reorganized all knowledge around observation and physical reason rather than religious authority. Published underground through commercial Swiss networks, banned and reprinted, read by the educated class across Europe and the American colonies. It established the framework governing Western intellectual life: measurable physical knowledge is real; everything else is superstition awaiting correction.

Why — the gain and control

The Encyclopédie was commercially published by merchants who stood to profit from a post-Church knowledge market. Its ideas served the rising commercial class wanting access to land, trade, and governance monopolized by the Church and aristocracy. Undermining religious authority was good for business. The secular scientific framework that replaced it was equally useful — it simply served a different set of powerful interests. Funded significantly by the European merchant capital described above.

Primary sources
  • Robert Darnton, The Business of Enlightenment (1979): the definitive account of the Encyclopédie's commercial production.

115cc3d6832046ca.h:
France, 1789–1799

French Revolution & Dechristianization

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

First government to attempt replacing the Church's definition of reality with state-enforced secular materialism

What they did

The revolutionary government's dechristianization campaign (1793–94) did not merely separate Church and State. It tried to replace the Church's framework for what humans are with a secular alternative — the Cult of Reason, then the Cult of the Supreme Being. Churches became Temples of Reason. The calendar was redesigned around nature and secular cycles. For the first time, a major state tried to install a secular, physical-world-only picture of human beings by government decree across an entire national population.

Why — the gain and control

It failed as a popular movement — the French peasantry kept their faith. But it established secular materialism as the intellectual framework of European progressive governance and provided the template that every subsequent revolutionary state drew on. The Soviet Union's approach was modeled directly on this — same logic, more power to enforce it. What looked like liberation from religious control was also the prototype for state control of metaphysical reality.

Primary sources
  • Michel Vovelle, The Revolution Against the Church (1991): documented the dechristianization campaign's methods.
  • Mona Ozouf, Festivals and the French Revolution (1988): analyzed the construction of secular substitutes for religious ceremony.
All connections

The Encyclopédie (documented), Soviet & CCP Ideological Apparatus (documented), Holbach's Salon (inferred), John Locke (inferred)

a10c04ad9f6876bb.h:
USSR/China/Global, 1917–1991

Soviet & CCP Ideological Apparatus

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

The first and largest state implementation of mandatory materialist ontology: dialectical materialism required by law across the USSR, China, and affiliated states — at peak, reaching over 1.5 billion people simultaneously

What they did

Lenin's Materialism and Empirio-criticism (1909) established dialectical materialism — the doctrine that only physical matter and the economic forces it generates are real — as mandatory state philosophy. The Communist Party of the Soviet Union then built three interlocking apparatus to enforce it:

The party apparatus (Comintern, political officers, censorship): every publication, academic paper, and public statement had to operate within dialectical materialist terms. Deviation was a political offense. The Comintern exported this mandate through affiliated communist parties across Europe, Asia, Latin America, and Africa.

The education system: Soviet and Chinese school curricula taught the physical-world-only framework through every subject. History was driven by material forces — class struggle and economic development — not ideas, spirits, or individuals. Psychology was behavior, not inner life. Religion was classified as false consciousness. At peak combined influence, this curriculum reached over 1.5 billion people simultaneously in the USSR, Eastern Europe, China, and Vietnam.

The CCP's cultural destruction: during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), traditional Chinese frameworks — Taoist, Confucian, and Buddhist cosmologies embedding humans in living relationships with nature, ancestors, and cosmic order — were classified as feudal superstition and actively destroyed. Texts were burned, practitioners imprisoned or killed. Three thousand years of living-world philosophy were targeted for systematic elimination within a generation.

Why — the gain and control

The Soviet and Western routes were political opposites — one demanded collective material struggle, the other individual market competition — but the underlying metaphysical claim was identical: humans are physical beings in a physical world, and the forces that matter are material ones. Two competing superpowers, presenting themselves as offering incompatible visions of humanity, agreed completely on what a human being fundamentally is. Their populations fought about politics while sharing the same metaphysical prison. The Soviet state understood this leverage explicitly: strip the sense that any dimension of human experience exceeds state power — spiritual, relational, ecological, ancestral — and you strip the vocabulary in which resistance beyond material terms can be articulated.

Primary sources
  • V.I. Lenin, Materialism and Empirio-criticism (1909): established dialectical materialism as the mandatory framework — primary source.
  • Sheila Fitzpatrick, Education and Social Mobility in the Soviet Union (1979): documented how the Soviet school system implemented the materialist worldview.
  • Perry Link, The Uses of Literature (2000): documented CCP management of cultural production to enforce the materialist framework.
  • Roderick MacFarquhar and Michael Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006): standard account of the Cultural Revolution's systematic destruction of traditional Chinese metaphysical frameworks.
All connections

French Revolution & Dechristianization (documented), Chicago School of Economics (convergence)

USSR/China/Global, 1917–1991

Soviet & CCP Ideological Apparatus

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

The first and largest state implementation of mandatory materialist ontology: dialectical materialism required by law across the USSR, China, and affiliated states — at peak, reaching over 1.5 billion people simultaneously

What they did

Lenin's Materialism and Empirio-criticism (1909) established dialectical materialism — the doctrine that only physical matter and the economic forces it generates are real — as mandatory state philosophy. The Communist Party of the Soviet Union then built three interlocking apparatus to enforce it:

The party apparatus (Comintern, political officers, censorship): every publication, academic paper, and public statement had to operate within dialectical materialist terms. Deviation was a political offense. The Comintern exported this mandate through affiliated communist parties across Europe, Asia, Latin America, and Africa.

The education system: Soviet and Chinese school curricula taught the physical-world-only framework through every subject. History was driven by material forces — class struggle and economic development — not ideas, spirits, or individuals. Psychology was behavior, not inner life. Religion was classified as false consciousness. At peak combined influence, this curriculum reached over 1.5 billion people simultaneously in the USSR, Eastern Europe, China, and Vietnam.

The CCP's cultural destruction: during the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), traditional Chinese frameworks — Taoist, Confucian, and Buddhist cosmologies embedding humans in living relationships with nature, ancestors, and cosmic order — were classified as feudal superstition and actively destroyed. Texts were burned, practitioners imprisoned or killed. Three thousand years of living-world philosophy were targeted for systematic elimination within a generation.

Why — the gain and control

The Soviet and Western routes were political opposites — one demanded collective material struggle, the other individual market competition — but the underlying metaphysical claim was identical: humans are physical beings in a physical world, and the forces that matter are material ones. Two competing superpowers, presenting themselves as offering incompatible visions of humanity, agreed completely on what a human being fundamentally is. Their populations fought about politics while sharing the same metaphysical prison. The Soviet state understood this leverage explicitly: strip the sense that any dimension of human experience exceeds state power — spiritual, relational, ecological, ancestral — and you strip the vocabulary in which resistance beyond material terms can be articulated.

eedbae46286bc904.h:
Germany, 1848–1880

Büchner & Scientific Materialists

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

First mass-market books telling working people: thought is what the brain does, as digestion is what the stomach does

What they did

Ludwig Büchner, Jakob Moleschott, and Carl Vogt were German medical doctors writing for ordinary readers after the failed 1848 revolutions. Büchner's Force and Matter (1855) went through 21 editions in 17 languages. Their message in plain terms: the soul does not exist. Thought is brain function, the same way digestion is stomach function. There is nothing about you that exceeds your physical body. This view — scientific materialism — was the first large-scale delivery of the physical-beings-in-a-physical-world framework to non-elite audiences.

Why — the gain and control

BÃ¼chner, Moleschott, and Vogt were writing for working-class readers with a specific political argument: if God and the soul are fictions maintained by priests and kings, then the Church's command to accept your suffering is fraud rather than divine will. This was genuine political liberation in that direction — it struck at clerical authority and the metaphysical foundation of the old regime. The intent was emancipatory.

The structural problem — which was not their intent — is that the same framework that dismantled one authority structure was immediately available for another. Strip the world of sacred relationships and inherent value, strip the person of soul and cosmic membership, and what you have left is a physical being in a physical world governed by natural forces. That is the framework Spencer arrived at by a completely different route (evolutionary biology, not anti-clerical medicine) and applied to economics and society. The convergence was structural rather than causal: two different projects arrived at the same ontological ground floor, and the industrial class that needed that ground floor was better positioned to operationalize it than the working-class audience that had first received it as liberation.

The transition was not immediate, and the connection was not intentional. The working-class materialism of the 1850s did not cause Spencer's Social Darwinism — Spencer was writing for a middle-class readership with opposite class interests. What the scientific materialists provided was an already-distributed framework that Spencer's audience had absorbed, making the "survival of the fittest" claim feel like it was confirming something already known rather than introducing something new.

Primary sources
  • Frederick Gregory, Scientific Materialism in Nineteenth-Century Germany (1977): the definitive account of the German scientific materialist movement.

beeec23ff5db30c8.h:
England, 1859–1882

Charles Darwin

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Demonstrated humans evolved from animals — making the materialist view scientifically established

What they did

Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) and The Descent of Man (1871) made the materialist view of humanity scientifically credible to educated people everywhere. Not design — selection. Not purpose — survival. Humans evolved from primates by the same blind process that shaped every other species. Darwin was cautious about the philosophical implications. The network around him was not. Voyage funded by British imperial capital (the Admiralty), specimen collections housed in Crown institutions.

Why — the gain and control

Darwin's theory did not itself endorse any political or economic system. But it was immediately adopted by the industrial class because it made their arrangement sound like nature. Competition, hierarchy, differential survival — these weren't cruelties of the new economic order. They were evolution. The theory's scientific authority gave this claim a legitimacy that no mere philosophy could provide. Darwin was uncomfortable with this use of his work. His discomfort was irrelevant to those who needed it.

Primary sources
  • Adrian Desmond & James Moore, Darwin (1991): documented Darwin's social context and the appropriation of his work for political purposes he found uncomfortable.
  • Robert Richards, Darwin and the Emergence of Evolutionary Theories of Mind and Behavior (1987): traced how Darwin's theory was extended into psychology and social theory.

f298845b5a840fee.h:
England, 1860–1900

T.H. Huxley + The X Club

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Nine scientists who coordinated monthly to place materialists in every important institutional position in British science

What they did

Thomas Henry Huxley formed a private dining club of nine scientists — the X Club — that met monthly to coordinate journal placements, prize committees, and university appointments. Their explicit goal: replace religious authority in British intellectual life with scientific naturalism — the position that the physical world is all there is and science is the only legitimate path to knowledge. They co-founded the journal Nature. Huxley lectured to working-class audiences hundreds of times, coining the word "agnostic" as a respectable alternative to religious belief. The X Club operated with the support of the British Imperial state, which funded their institutional positions.

Why — the gain and control

Nine men understood that controlling what institutions officially endorse is more effective than winning arguments. They didn't debate religious believers — they outmaneuvered them institutionally. Within a generation, scientific naturalism was the standard in British universities. Through the British Empire's educational apparatus, it became the standard in universities from Calcutta to Nairobi to Sydney. The nine men of the X Club shifted the official definition of reality for populations they would never meet.

Primary sources
  • Ruth Barton, The X Club: Power and Authority in Victorian Science (2018): the first full account of the X Club's membership, coordination, and institutional strategy.
  • Paul White, Thomas Huxley: Making the 'Man of Science' (2003): documented Huxley's public role in constructing the cultural authority of science.

47da325958e2c7f7.h:
England/USA, 1860–1900

Herbert Spencer

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Coined 'survival of the fittest' — built a total philosophy that said competition and domination are the law of the universe

What they did

Spencer coined "survival of the fittest" (not Darwin) and constructed a total philosophical system applying evolutionary competition to every domain: biology, psychology, economics, society. His argument: the struggle between individuals, with the strong winning and the weak perishing, is not just what happens — it is the law of progress. Helping the weak violates cosmic law. He was the best-selling philosopher in the English-speaking world for two decades. His American lecture tour was funded by Carnegie and Rockefeller, who distributed his books at scale.

Why — the gain and control

Carnegie and Rockefeller funded Spencer's American tour because his framework did what no amount of lobbying could do: it made their monopolistic practices sound like natural law, made their workers' poverty sound like evolution working correctly, and made any demand for collective action or public welfare sound like a violation of nature. Spencer's ideas were an investment in public compliance that paid returns measured in generations of anti-labor, anti-regulation political culture.

Primary sources
  • Mark Francis, Herbert Spencer and the Invention of Modern Life (2007): the most complete account of Spencer's intellectual system and reception.
  • Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944): documented the American reception and industrial funding.

e22cdc4a842aad81.h:
Germany, 1870–1920

Ernst Haeckel + Monist League

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

500,000 copies of 'humans are just matter' — then 42,000 members spreading it door to door

What they did

Ernst Haeckel was Germany's most popular scientist. The Riddle of the Universe (1899) sold half a million copies and was translated into 25 languages. He then founded the German Monist League — 42,000 dues-paying members in local chapters. Their mission: replace every spiritual and religious understanding of human beings with a unified physical-only view as the basis for modern civilization. They published, lectured, and organized youth groups.

Why — the gain and control

The Monist League was the first mass-membership organization specifically designed to spread the physical-beings-in-a-physical-world framework to ordinary people. Its 42,000 members were shopkeepers, teachers, doctors, and workers who held public lectures and distributed literature across Germany — then the world's most literate country. The framework they spread was later available to the Nazi movement, which Haeckel did not intend, but which was available in his framework because it had dismantled every basis for human value that exceeded biological classification.

Primary sources
  • Daniel Gasman, The Scientific Origins of National Socialism (1971): traced the connection between Haeckel's monism and the ideological foundations of National Socialism.
  • Paul Weindling, Health, Race and German Politics (1989): documented the Monist League's influence on German public health and racial science.
All connections

30447fd94183b759.h:
Europe, 1848–1900

Workers' Press & Popular Science

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Cheap publications that first delivered 'you are just matter' to non-elite audiences as political liberation

What they did

Cheap printing made possible a flood of popular science publications in the second half of the 1800s. Workers' education institutes and mechanics' clubs provided the audience. These publications translated academic materialist arguments into plain language for artisans, factory workers, and shopkeepers. The framework arrived packaged as political liberation: if the soul is a fiction, then aristocratic and clerical authority is fraud.

Why — the gain and control

The working-class person receiving this was getting genuine intellectual tools alongside an invisible installation: the same framework that dismantled divine authority also dismantled sacred community, sacred land, and sacred relationship with the natural world. The liberation from one form of control came with a pre-installed vulnerability to the next. The industrial class that arrived immediately after with "survival of the fittest" found an audience already primed to hear human struggle as natural law.

Primary sources
  • Andreas Daum, Wissenschaftspopularisierung im 19. Jahrhundert (1998): documented the German popular science movement and its relationship to working-class politics.

835a1e0c9e8da0cb.h:
Global, 1869–present

Scientific Journals & Popular Science Press

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Nature, Scientific American — made scientific authority the only legitimate authority, making non-physical questions unpublishable

What they did

The X Club co-founded Nature in 1869. The popular science press — Scientific American and its equivalents — translated scientific authority into mass culture. The implicit message in every issue: this is how reality works, determined by physical measurement. Spiritual, philosophical, or participatory accounts of reality don't appear in these pages — not because they were debated and lost, but because they were defined out of the category of knowledge these journals adjudicate.

Why — the gain and control

Scientific journals operate on the same authority structure as the institutions around them: peer review, institutional affiliation, measurable results. The authority of this system grew throughout the 20th century into an essentially unchallengeable cultural force. Any claim to knowledge that cannot be verified through this system — about consciousness, meaning, spiritual experience, or participatory relationship with the natural world — is excluded by structural definition. The system doesn't argue against these claims. It simply doesn't have a category for them.

Primary sources
  • Ruth Barton, "'Huxley, Lubbock, and Half a Dozen Others'" (Isis, 1998): documented the founding of Nature and its role in constructing scientific authority.

c6f1ede19a23d26e.h:
USA, 1880–1940

American Newspaper Empires

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Pulitzer, Hearst — mass-circulation papers that normalized 'survival of the fittest' as common sense for millions daily

What they did

By 1900 the American newspaper industry reached more people daily than any prior communication system in history. Pulitzer's New York World hit one million daily circulation by 1898; Hearst's chain eventually spanned 28 papers in 18 cities. Both chains were owned by men whose editorial instincts were shaped by their class interests and their reading of Spencer. But the deeper mechanism was structural: the newspaper was the first technology that delivered a consistent worldview — the same framing, the same categories, the same background assumptions — to millions of readers simultaneously, every morning.

What those readers encountered daily: the wealthy framed as natural achievers, poverty framed as personal failure, labor disputes framed as obstruction of natural economic processes, Carnegie and Rockefeller profiled as exemplars of what intelligent competition produces. The New York Times ran editorials explicitly citing Spencer in 1882 against labor reform legislation. Hearst's papers editorially opposed every major piece of labor protection legislation from 1900 to 1935 (Michael McGerr, A Fierce Discontent, 2003). The Associated Press wire service — which supplied most American newspapers with national content — was controlled by a self-selecting board of member newspapers whose membership rules kept out competitors and concentrated the production of "neutral" news in a small class of owners (Melville Stone, AP managing director 1893–1921, documented in Richard Schwarzlose, The Nation's Newsbrokers, 1990).

Why — the gain and control

The newspaper's power was not that it argued for Social Darwinism. It was that Social Darwinism became the invisible premise of what news looked like. A framework declared as ideology can be challenged; a framework operating as the background grammar of description cannot. When every crime story implies poverty as moral failing, every business story implies wealth as natural merit, and every labor story implies market disruption as the category of concern — those assumptions are not being argued. They are being rehearsed, daily, until they feel like the structure of reality itself.

The documented ownership connection matters: Pulitzer and Hearst were not incidentally wealthy men who owned papers. They were class actors who understood the press as both commercial asset and cultural weapon. Carnegie & Rockefeller Network

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Built the University of Chicago — training the economists who ran the 20th century

What they did

Carnegie and Rockefeller funded Spencer's lecture tours, distributed his books, and funded the newspapers that spread his ideas to mass audiences. Rockefeller's founding gift to the University of Chicago in 1890 specified economics as a central department. That institution became the training ground for Milton Friedman, Friedrich Hayek, and the entire Chicago School — which produced the economists who ran the IMF, designed Structural Adjustment Programs, and trained finance ministers across 70 countries. Directly funded by the American Industrial Capital class.

Why — the gain and control

Carnegie ran monopolies while publicly citing open competition as cosmic law. Rockefeller's private letters show a man who ran an engineered industrial system while publicly framing it as natural selection. The investment in Spencer's ideas and the University of Chicago was the purchase of a moral framework that made their practices look like physics. The return, measured across the 20th century in regulatory immunity and policy alignment, was the highest-ROI investment either man ever made.

Primary sources
  • Ron Chernow, Titan: The Life of John D. Rockefeller Sr. (1998).
  • Philip Mirowski, Never Let a Serious Crisis Go to Waste (2013): traced the Chicago School's lineage from Rockefeller's founding gift.

e962204d345f0589.h:
Austria, 1924–1938

Vienna Circle

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Declared questions about non-physical reality not just wrong, but meaningless — closing the debate permanently

What they did

A group of philosophers and scientists in Vienna met weekly from 1924 to 1936. Their move — the most decisive in this entire history — was not to argue against spiritual or non-material views of reality. They declared those questions to be grammatical errors. "Does the soul survive death?" is not false, they said. It is meaningless — like asking whether green weighs more than Thursday. Only physically testable statements have meaning at all. This position — logical positivism — immunized the physical-world-only view against philosophical challenge: you can't argue against it because challenging it means you're not playing a legitimate game.

Why — the gain and control

The Vienna Circle's members were mostly Jewish, progressive, anti-fascist intellectuals who fled to America when the Nazis rose. Their intent was liberation from dogma. But the framework they installed — that non-physical questions are literally nonsense — functioned as the most complete philosophical gatekeeping in history. Once this framework occupied the philosophy departments of Oxford, Harvard, Chicago, and their global satellites, the university system could no longer seriously ask whether humans were more than their biology. The question was definitionally off the table.

Primary sources
  • David Edmonds & John Eidinow, Wittgenstein's Poker (2001): documented the Vienna Circle's social world and the institutional spread of logical positivism.
  • A.J. Ayer, Language, Truth and Logic (1936): the document that spread logical positivism to English-speaking universities.

32fd655823267f34.h:
USA, 1936–1960

Carnap at Chicago & American Diaspora

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Vienna Circle refugees took over American philosophy departments — making non-physical questions professionally unspeakable

What they did

Rudolf Carnap went to the University of Chicago. Hans Reichenbach went to UCLA. Herbert Feigl went to Minnesota. Each trained the graduate students who became the professors now teaching. A.J. Ayer attended Vienna Circle meetings, returned to Oxford, and wrote Language, Truth and Logic (1936) — required undergraduate reading across Britain and the Commonwealth. The framework they carried: any statement about reality that cannot be empirically tested is literally meaningless. Funding for this diaspora's academic positions came significantly from US Cold War national security sources.

Why — the gain and control

This was not a coordinated conspiracy — these men fled for their lives. But the framework they installed in elite universities served a specific long-term function: it made the secular, competitive-individual, matter-is-all worldview the only one that educated professionals were trained to take seriously. Anyone who raised questions about meaning, spirit, or participatory relationship with the world was, by this framework's own definition, confused. The framework protected the status quo by making its philosophical alternatives literally unspeakable in educated company.

Primary sources
  • George Reisch, How the Cold War Transformed Philosophy of Science (2005): documented how Cold War politics shaped the reception and spread of logical positivism.

England, 1936–1970

Ayer at Oxford & British Academy

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Spread Vienna Circle's rule through British and all Commonwealth universities

What they did

Ayer's Language, Truth and Logic became the standard introductory philosophy text in British universities — and through the Commonwealth system in Indian, African, Australian, and Canadian universities. Oxford under Ayer and his successors was the most prestigious philosophy department in the English-speaking world, its framework the global standard for what philosophy was permitted to do. Generations of students from Lagos to Delhi to Sydney received their only formal exposure to questions about the nature of mind and reality within a framework that classified non-material questions as confused.

Why — the gain and control

The one or two philosophy courses a doctor, lawyer, engineer, or journalist takes during their education is the moment when they receive their only formal engagement with questions about the nature of human beings and reality. When those courses operate within a framework that classifies non-physical questions as grammatical errors, those future professionals carry that classification for life — not as a philosophy they chose, but as the background assumption of what educated people believe. Oxford's global reach made this the professional-class default across the former British Empire.

abf7c8b748cae97b.h:
Global, 1950–present

Anglo-American Philosophy Departments

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Trained every educated person's one or two philosophy courses — worldwide

What they did

After the Vienna Circle diaspora, analytic philosophy — operating on the assumption that only physically testable statements are meaningful — became the dominant framework in British and American philosophy departments, and through their global influence, in universities worldwide. These departments trained the professors who taught the required philosophy courses in every field — medicine, law, engineering, economics. Questions about consciousness, meaning, and the relationship between self and world were not resolved. They were reclassified as technically confused.

Why — the gain and control

The university system is the most effective delivery mechanism for professional-class worldviews ever constructed. What the philosophy department decides counts as a real question shapes what questions the medical, legal, and political systems ever think to ask. When the foundational philosophical training of every educated professional globally operates within a framework that dismisses non-material experience as nonsense, that framework becomes the invisible operating assumption of every institution those professionals build. The professors who taught these courses did not understand themselves as suppressing alternatives — they understood themselves as doing rigorous philosophy. The exclusion of non-physical questions was framed as intellectual maturity, not gatekeeping. That this framing served specific interests is documented in retrospect by scholars including Charles Taylor (Sources of the Self, 1989) and Hilary Putnam (Renewing Philosophy, 1992); it was not the self-understanding of most practitioners.

The endpoint this tradition produced — documented in the Churchlands' work at UCSD from the 1980s onward — was eliminative materialism: not that consciousness is physical, but that consciousness as ordinarily understood does not exist, and will be replaced by neuroscientific vocabulary when the science is complete. Patricia Churchland's Neurophilosophy (1986) and Paul Churchland's Scientific Realism and the Plasticity of Mind (1979) became the default framework in philosophy of mind across North American departments. Van Inwagen's mereological nihilism (tables don't exist; only particles arranged table-wise) and Unger's eliminativism about ordinary objects represent the tradition carried to its logical conclusion — technically sophisticated arguments that reached almost no one outside graduate seminars, but which document where the underlying premises lead when followed rigorously.

Primary sources
  • Scott Soames, Philosophical Analysis in the Twentieth Century (2003): documented the spread of analytic philosophy as the global default.

868b84ce5cc756a3.h:
Global, 1950–present

Anglo-American Philosophy Departments

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Trained every educated person's one or two philosophy courses — worldwide

What they did

After the Vienna Circle diaspora, analytic philosophy — operating on the assumption that only physically testable statements are meaningful — became the dominant framework in British and American philosophy departments, and through their global influence, in universities worldwide. These departments trained the professors who taught the required philosophy courses in every field — medicine, law, engineering, economics. Questions about consciousness, meaning, and the relationship between self and world were not resolved. They were reclassified as technically confused.

Why — the gain and control

The university system is the most effective delivery mechanism for professional-class worldviews ever constructed. What the philosophy department decides counts as a real question shapes what questions the medical, legal, and political systems ever think to ask. When the foundational philosophical training of every educated professional globally operates within a framework that dismisses non-material experience as nonsense, that framework becomes the invisible operating assumption of every institution those professionals build. The professors who taught these courses did not understand themselves as suppressing alternatives — they understood themselves as doing rigorous philosophy. The exclusion of non-physical questions was framed as intellectual maturity, not gatekeeping. That this framing served specific interests is documented in retrospect by scholars including Charles Taylor (Sources of the Self, 1989) and Hilary Putnam (Renewing Philosophy, 1992); it was not the self-understanding of most practitioners.

The endpoint this tradition produced — documented in the Churchlands' work at UCSD from the 1980s onward — was eliminative materialism: not that consciousness is physical, but that consciousness as ordinarily understood does not exist, and will be replaced by neuroscientific vocabulary when the science is complete. Patricia Churchland's Neurophilosophy (1986) and Paul Churchland's Scientific Realism and the Plasticity of Mind (1979) became the default framework in philosophy of mind across North American departments. Van Inwagen's mereological nihilism (tables don't exist; only particles arranged table-wise) and Unger's eliminativism about ordinary objects represent the tradition carried to its logical conclusion — technically sophisticated arguments that reached almost no one outside graduate seminars, but which document where the underlying premises lead when followed rigorously.

d328eb29abb6df3d.h:
Prussia/Global, 1717–present

Prussian & Global School System

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

First compulsory school system — designed around military drill and individual ranked performance, copied by the entire world

What they did

Prussia instituted compulsory schooling in 1717, designed around military discipline: individual ranked performance, obedience to authority, age segregation. Fichte's Addresses to the German Nation (1807) provided the explicit goal: schools must form desire itself before the child can question it, producing a self that wants what the state and economy need. Horace Mann brought the model to America in the 1840s after visiting Prussian schools. It spread through the British Empire. Every compulsory school system on earth today descends from this model.

Why — the gain and control

The physical structure of the school — individual desks in rows, individual grading, bell schedules replacing natural rhythms, abstract symbolic knowledge replacing embodied experience — installs the isolated-individual relationship to the world not through teaching but through the physical fact of every day of childhood. Twelve years of that structure produces an adult for whom the isolated-individual experience is simply what reality feels like. No ideology required. The architecture delivers the message.

Primary sources
  • John Taylor Gatto, The Underground History of American Education (2001): documented the Prussian origin of the American school system.
  • Johann Gottlieb Fichte, Addresses to the German Nation (1807): the primary source text for the explicit goals of compulsory schooling.

62d797109133975b.h:
USA/Global, 1950–1990

Chicago School of Economics

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Trained the economists who ran the world's governments — embedding 'humans are naturally self-interested competitors' as economic science

What they did

The University of Chicago Economics Department — built around Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, initially funded by the Volker Fund, then by the Koch and Scaife networks — trained a generation whose graduates became finance ministers, central bank governors, and IMF directors globally. The "Chicago Boys" pipeline ran in Chile, Argentina, Bolivia, Poland, and Russia: economists were trained in a single worldview and returned to implement it as government policy. The Mont Pelerin Society (1947) coordinated this network internationally. Funded directly by both American Industrial Capital and Cold War national security apparatus.

Why — the gain and control

Charles Koch's internal documents describe political and academic funding as investment with measurable returns in specific regulatory outcomes. The funding of Chicago School infrastructure was not ideological philanthropy — it was the purchase of the training pipeline that produced the officials who would deregulate, privatize, and restructure the material conditions of hundreds of millions of people according to a framework that treated humans as naturally self-interested individual competitors. That framework happened to align with the economic interests of the industries whose executives funded it. Neither Friedman nor most Chicago economists understood themselves as ontological engineers. Friedman explicitly presented his work as the discovery of natural economic laws — the same epistemological move as physics — not as the construction of a worldview. The claim embedded in that framework (that humans are by nature self-interested competing individuals, and any other description is sentimentality) was presented as discovered truth. The ontological effect — on what populations understood themselves to be — was real regardless of the framing. The Chicago-trained economists who staffed the IMF and World Bank from the 1980s extended this pipeline globally: structural adjustment loan conditionality imposed the Chicago framework on indebted nations across Africa, Latin America, and Asia as a technical requirement of sound economic management. The Chicago-trained economists who staffed the IMF and World Bank from the 1980s extended this pipeline globally: structural adjustment loan conditionality imposed the Chicago framework on indebted nations across Africa, Latin America, and Asia as a technical requirement of "sound economic management."

Primary sources
  • Philip Mirowski, Never Let a Serious Crisis Go to Waste (2013): the most comprehensive account of the Chicago School's funding and policy influence.
  • Naomi Klein, The Shock Doctrine (2007): documented the Chicago Boys pipelines in Chile, Argentina, and Eastern Europe.

da1bbff10fe25e4d.h:
Global, 1975–2010

Science Bestseller Network

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Dawkins, Dennett, Pinker — translated 'you are only your brain' into mass-market books read by tens of millions

What they did

A relay of science writers delivered the academic framework to mass audiences: Richard Dawkins's The Selfish Gene (1976) — you are a survival machine built by genes. Steven Pinker's How the Mind Works (1997). Antonio Damasio's Descartes' Error (1994). Daniel Dennett's Consciousness Explained (1991) — there is no inner observer; consciousness is just what the brain does, and the self is a story the brain tells itself. Translated into dozens of languages, sold in tens of millions of copies. These books arrived in airports and bookstores as science, not philosophy. Published by conglomerates significantly funded by Postwar Corporate capital.

Why — the gain and control

For publishers, these books were lucrative properties in a reliable market: educated secular readers who wanted scientific confirmation of their worldview. For the network as a whole, they delivered the "you are only your body and its processes" view to the global educated professional class as established science — not a position being argued but what has already been proven. A person who takes these books seriously finds that any felt sense of connection beyond their physical body is, by scientific definition, an illusion their brain is running. These authors understood themselves as correcting public misunderstanding of what science has established, not as spreading a metaphysical framework. They believed they were describing reality accurately. The philosophical claim embedded in that description — that consciousness is computational, the self a narrative fiction, altruism gene propagation — is a complete metaphysics presented as established science. The gap between those two framings is documented in Thomas Nagel's Mind and Cosmos (2012) and Mary Midgley's Science as Salvation (1992).

Primary sources
  • David Kaiser & W. Patrick McCray (eds.), Groovy Science (2016): documented the cultural context of 1970s–2000s popular science.

03f12ba51ccc2b50.h:
Global, 1835–1960

British Empire Education System

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Macaulay's policy: replace all indigenous knowledge systems worldwide with Western education

What they did

Macaulay's 1835 Minute on Indian Education stated the goal plainly: produce people "Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect." Implemented across India, Africa, the Caribbean, Southeast Asia, and the Pacific. The curriculum was Western secular science and English literature. Indigenous knowledge systems — which typically embedded humans in living relationship with land, ancestors, and community — were classified as primitive superstition. Access to any employment in the colonial administration required operating entirely within Western frameworks. Funded and deployed directly by the British Imperial State.

Why — the gain and control

The economic logic was documented by its architects: a population educated in Western categories would administer the empire in Western categories, maintain Western legal frameworks protecting colonial property rights, and require fewer British personnel. But the deeper function was epistemological: a people who understand themselves and their world through the colonizer's framework cannot easily articulate resistance in terms that exceed that framework. The destruction of indigenous ways of knowing was not incidental to colonial extraction. It was the psychological infrastructure that made extraction sustainable across generations.

Primary sources
  • Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Decolonising the Mind (1986): primary account of how British colonial education dismantled African ways of knowing.
  • Gauri Viswanathan, Masks of Conquest (1989): documented how English literary education functioned as ideological apparatus in British India.

70b5ce7f24678704.h:
England, 1651

Thomas Hobbes

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Derived a complete political philosophy from purely materialist premises: humans are competitive matter in motion, life without sovereign power is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'

What they did

Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) made the foundational argument that reduced humans to mechanistic matter in motion. In his "state of nature" — humans without government — life is a "war of all against all" because every person is driven purely by appetite, aversion, and the desire for self-preservation. There is no natural community, no inherent moral order, no sacred relationship between people and the world they inhabit. Only the sovereign's power, backed by force, prevents mutual destruction. He explicitly stated: "the condition of man... is a condition of war of every one against every one." This was the first systematic derivation of a complete political philosophy from purely materialist premises — humans as competitive atoms who require imposed order or market coordination to prevent destroying each other.

The possessive individualism framework — the political theory that free individuals own themselves as property — was explicitly mapped by C.B. Macpherson in 1962 as originating in Hobbes, developed by Locke, and becoming the foundational assumption of market society. Every subsequent argument that "human nature is competitive" traces directly to Hobbes's state of nature as its philosophical anchor.

Why — the gain and control

Hobbes was writing in the aftermath of the English Civil War with a specific political purpose: justify absolute sovereignty to prevent civil chaos. But the metaphysical framework he deployed — humans as naturally competitive, self-interested, materialist units — was immediately available for every subsequent actor who needed to claim that competitive individualism is natural rather than constructed. Three centuries later, neoliberal economists presented Hobbes's state of nature as scientific anthropology. Milton Friedman's model of the self-interested individual, public choice theory's model of the self-interested politician, and Ayn Rand's model of the sovereign self all rest on the Hobbesian baseline. The documented chain: Macpherson's Political Theory of Possessive Individualism (1962) traced the lineage explicitly; Friedman cited Hobbes's possessive individualism framework in his Chicago seminars.

Primary sources
  • Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651), Ch. XIII: 'the condition of man is a condition of war of every one against every one' — primary source.
  • C.B. Macpherson, The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism (1962): the canonical scholarly analysis tracing how Hobbes and Locke built the philosophical foundation for market society.
  • Leo Strauss, The Political Philosophy of Hobbes (1936): documented Hobbes as the founder of modern liberal political philosophy based on self-interest.
All connections

aa743c2a407bb334.h:
France, 1830–1842

Auguste Comte & Positivism

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

Founded positivism — declared that only scientifically verifiable knowledge is legitimate, institutionalizing the exclusion of metaphysics as a named philosophical movement for the first time

What they did

Comte's six-volume Course of Positive Philosophy (1830–1842) founded positivism: the doctrine that knowledge passes through three stages — theological, metaphysical, and positive (scientific) — with the positive stage being the final, correct form of understanding. Only what can be empirically observed, measured, and verified through the scientific method constitutes legitimate knowledge. Everything else — spiritual claims, metaphysical assertions, felt meaning, participatory relationship with the natural world — is not merely unverified but pre-scientific, a lower form of understanding humanity must leave behind. He proposed replacing religion with a "Religion of Humanity" centered on scientific knowledge and secular progress.

The Vienna Circle explicitly cited Comte as their intellectual precursor. Logical positivism is Comte with symbolic logic added — the same core operation: define the boundary of legitimate knowledge in a way that excludes non-physical claims by structural definition rather than argument.

Why — the gain and control

Comte's positivism gave the exclusion of non-physical reality its first systematic philosophical name and institutional form. Before Comte, dismissing metaphysics was a position; after Comte, it was a movement with a name, a history, and a theory of intellectual progress. This framing — that eliminating metaphysics is progress, not loss — is the ideological move that made the Vienna Circle's later work feel like the completion of a long intellectual arc rather than an aggressive philosophical claim. The documented chain: the Vienna Circle's founding manifesto (1929) explicitly lists Comte alongside Mach, Russell, and Frege as intellectual predecessors. A.J. Ayer's Language, Truth and Logic (1936), which spread logical positivism through British and Commonwealth universities, traces its lineage directly to Comtean positivism.

Primary sources
  • Auguste Comte, Course of Positive Philosophy (1830–42): primary source establishing the three-stage law and the definition of positivism.
  • Vienna Circle, 'The Scientific Conception of the World: The Vienna Circle' (1929 manifesto): explicitly names Comte as founding intellectual predecessor.
  • Leszek Kolakowski, The Alienation of Reason: A History of Positivist Thought (1968): the standard scholarly history tracing positivism from Comte to logical positivism.
