0f7fafa67ba22d66.h:
USA (Yale), 1872–1910

William Graham Sumner

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Yale professor who translated Spencer's Social Darwinism into American academic sociology — 'the millionaires are a product of natural selection'; poverty is evolution in action; redistribution violates natural law

What they did

Yale professor William Graham Sumner was the American academic who installed Spencer's Social Darwinism into U.S. university curricula with professional legitimacy. What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883) argued the answer explicitly: nothing. The poor are poor because they are less fit; the rich are rich because they are more fit; any redistribution violates natural law. In his lecture "The Challenge of Facts" he stated: "The millionaires are a product of natural selection, acting on the whole body of men to pick out those who can meet the requirement of certain work to be done." His Folkways (1906) became a founding text of American sociology. He coined the terms "ethnocentrism" and "in-group/out-group" while simultaneously arguing that competitive struggle — between individuals and nations — was the mechanism of progress.

As a Yale professor from 1872 to 1910, Sumner trained the generation of American sociologists, economists, and public intellectuals who built their disciplines' foundational assumptions. Spencer was British and abstract; Sumner gave the same framework American academic legitimacy, university course credit, and the authority of a Yale chair.

Why — the gain and control

The material interest served by Sumner's framework was identical to Spencer's: it made the industrial monopolies of Carnegie and Rockefeller look like evolution rather than political economy. Sumner was aware of this. He corresponded with Carnegie and explicitly defended the concentration of wealth as natural selection producing the most capable stewards of capital. Carnegie in turn cited Sumner in his own writings. Documented chain: Richard Hofstadter's Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944) — the standard scholarly account — documents in detail how Sumner's framework provided academic legitimacy for the Gilded Age industrial class's self-justifications.

Primary sources
  • William Graham Sumner, What Social Classes Owe to Each Other (1883): primary source — explicit argument that redistribution violates natural law.
  • William Graham Sumner, 'The Challenge of Facts' (1914): 'The millionaires are a product of natural selection' — primary source for the core claim.
  • Richard Hofstadter, Social Darwinism in American Thought (1944): the standard scholarly account of how this framework served Gilded Age economic interests.

bd3e281b0783fa9b.h:
USA (Virginia/GMU), 1962–2013

James Buchanan & Public Choice

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Public choice theory applied 'humans are only self-interested' to politics itself, systematically delegitimizing every form of collective democratic action — developed at Koch-funded institutions, Nobel Prize 1986

What they did

Buchanan's public choice theory — developed at the University of Virginia and George Mason University with direct Koch funding — applied the "humans are only self-interested" axiom to political actors themselves. Politicians, regulators, and bureaucrats are not public servants motivated by the common good; they are self-interested utility maximizers gaming the system for personal gain. Every regulatory agency is captured. Every public program is rent-seeking. Every collective decision is the aggregation of individual self-interest, which means democratic majorities can be used by organized interests to extract resources from unorganized ones. His Calculus of Consent (1962, with Gordon Tullock) and Limits of Liberty (1975) provided the theoretical framework. Nobel Prize in Economics, 1986.

The philosophical operation is the most complete in this network's history. Spencer applied "survival of the fittest" to society. Public choice applied "pure self-interest" to government itself. Once accepted, the framework makes it structurally impossible to articulate a legitimate form of collective democratic action — because every such action is, by definition, the expression of self-interest by some group at others' expense.

Why — the gain and control

Nancy MacLean's Democracy in Chains (2017) documented, using Buchanan's own archive at George Mason University, that Charles Koch specifically selected Buchanan as the intellectual whose framework could most effectively neutralize democratic constraints on market power. Koch funded Buchanan's Center for Study of Public Choice for decades. The goal, documented in Koch's own strategy papers, was to use public choice theory to shift the regulatory environment — Koch wanted specific deregulatory policy outcomes. Buchanan's own stated goal was scientific: he believed he was applying rigorous economic reasoning to political behavior and discovering how government actually works. Neither framed the project as eliminating a non-materialist conception of human beings. The ontological effect — public choice provides a complete account of political behavior in which any motivation beyond self-interest appears as naive or dishonest — was the framework's logical consequence, not its stated purpose. The documented chain is unusually clear: funding source, intellectual product, policy outcome, and the principals' own words are all on record (MacLean, 2017).

Primary sources
  • James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock, Calculus of Consent (1962): foundational text of public choice theory — primary source.
  • Nancy MacLean, Democracy in Chains: The Deep History of the Radical Right's Stealth Plan for America (2017): uses Buchanan's Koch-funded archive to document the strategic relationship.
  • Charles Koch, internal strategy documents (released through litigation): describe the 20-year plan to use academic funding to shift political foundations — cited in Mayer's Dark Money.

082d0fd4772a5937.h:
USA (Chicago), 1964–2014

Gary Becker Human Capital

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Extended rational-choice economic modeling to all of human life — family, crime, education, marriage — reframing every relationship as capital investment; completed the reduction of human existence to individual self-interest calculation

What they did

Becker extended rational-choice economic modeling to every domain of human life that had previously been understood as outside economics. Human Capital (1964) reframed education, skills, and personal development as investment decisions made by self-interested individuals maximizing lifetime earnings. A Treatise on the Family (1981) modeled marriage, children, and family structure as utility-maximizing choices. His work on crime framed criminal behavior as rational calculation of expected costs and benefits. Social relationships, personal bonds, even health decisions were recast as forms of capital accumulation. The framework was named homo economicus extended to its logical conclusion: every dimension of human life is a market. Nobel Prize in Economics, 1992.

This was not a value-neutral academic exercise. Becker was at the University of Chicago, trained by Milton Friedman, and his framework was the Chicago School's extension of market logic into the last domains it had not yet colonized: the family, the self, the interior life.

Why — the gain and control

Becker understood himself as extending the rigor of economic analysis into domains previously left to sociology and psychology — he described his work as scientific, not ideological. The framework he built carries a complete ontological picture: every human relationship becomes a cost-benefit calculation, every life decision portfolio optimization, every social institution a market equilibrium. The claim that this describes how things are rather than stakes a philosophical position about what humans fundamentally are is precisely the move that makes it effective. Human capital theory completed what Descartes began. If Descartes made the self an isolated observer, Becker made every relationship that self has into an investment portfolio. Children are human capital. Friendships are social capital. Love is a long-term utility calculation. 2d017d03fee1ca83.h:
London, 1955–present

Institute of Economic Affairs

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Founded on Hayek's explicit advice — the model that every subsequent market-liberal think tank worldwide was built on; directly shaped Thatcherism and became the template for 500+ Atlas-affiliated institutes globally

What they did

The IEA was founded in London in 1955 by Antony Fisher, after Friedrich Hayek specifically advised him that changing the climate of opinion through ideas — not entering politics — was the effective strategy. Fisher had read The Road to Serfdom and wrote to Hayek asking what to do. Hayek's response, documented in Fisher's own writings: found a scholarly institute, not a political party. Maintain charitable status. Publish ideas in academic form. Move the Overton window. The IEA published Hayek, Friedman, and Austrian School economists in accessible form for British audiences from the late 1950s. Keith Joseph — Margaret Thatcher's intellectual mentor — credited the IEA as the primary influence on the Thatcherite program. Thatcher herself visited the IEA regularly before taking power.

The IEA's key innovation was the separation of ideological advocacy from academic appearance. By publishing "scholarly" research rather than lobbying documents, it maintained charitable tax status while producing material that was directly used in political campaigns. This separation of form (academic) from function (advocacy) became the template for every think tank in the network.

Why — the gain and control

The IEA's significance is not primarily its own influence but its role as the explicit model for the global franchise. Antony Fisher went on to found the Atlas Economic Research Foundation (1981) specifically to replicate the IEA model worldwide. Fisher described the strategy in his own writings: Hayek's advice was the founding insight, the IEA was the proof of concept, and Atlas was the scaling mechanism. Documented chain: Richard Cockett's Thinking the Unthinkable (1994), based on IEA archives, is the standard scholarly history of how the IEA shaped British economic policy. The IEA's influence on Thatcher is documented in her own memoirs and Joseph's papers.

Primary sources
  • Richard Cockett, Thinking the Unthinkable: Think Tanks and the Economic Counter-Revolution, 1931–83 (1994): standard history based on IEA archives.
  • Antony Fisher, Must History Repeat Itself? (1974): Fisher's own account of Hayek's advice and the founding strategy.
  • Keith Joseph, speech at IEA's 40th anniversary (1995): credited IEA as primary intellectual influence on Thatcherism — primary source.
  • Margaret Thatcher, The Downing Street Years (1993): describes IEA's influence on her political development.

45e3010d92378d06.h:

Law & Economics Movement

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Olin Foundation spent $68 million to insert market-efficiency reasoning into law schools — Harvard, Yale, Chicago; federal judges sent to Koch-funded economics boot camps; by 1999, over 40% of sitting federal judges had attended

What they did

The law-and-economics movement inserted market-efficiency reasoning into judicial interpretation, legal education, and constitutional theory. The Olin Foundation spent over $68 million specifically targeting law schools — Harvard, Yale, Chicago, Virginia, Georgetown — to fund chairs, journals, and programs teaching that legal rules should be evaluated by their economic efficiency. The core doctrine: rights should be allocated to whoever values them most as determined by willingness to pay; the common law has always tended toward economically efficient outcomes; regulation should be evaluated by cost-benefit analysis using market prices as the measure of value.

Federal judges were sent to economics "boot camps" — the Law and Economics Center at George Mason University (Koch-funded) and similar programs at Chicago and Miami — at no cost to attendees, with transportation and accommodation covered. Between 1976 and 1999, over 40% of sitting federal judges attended these programs, according to research published in the Stanford Law Review. Robert Bork's The Antitrust Paradox (1978), the first major output of the movement, redefined antitrust law around consumer welfare (measured by price) rather than corporate power, directly enabling the merger waves of the 1980s and 1990s.

Why — the gain and control

The Olin Foundation stated goal — documented in its own records — was to counter "anti-business bias" in law schools and courts. Koch's stated goal was specific deregulatory outcomes. Neither framed the project as ontological engineering. What they funded was an analytical framework presenting market-efficiency reasoning as value-neutral legal science — the same epistemological move as logical positivism applied to law. The ontological assumption embedded in that framework (that market prices are the neutral measure of value, that willingness to pay legitimately arbitrates rights, that collective democratic preferences constitute "rent-seeking") was presented as economic rigor. A judge trained in this framework reaches systematically different outcomes on regulatory, antitrust, and property cases — not because instructed to, but because the framework's premises determine its conclusions. Documented chain: Steven Teles's Rise of the Conservative Legal Movement (2008) is the standard scholarly account. The judge-training programs were documented in detail by the New York Times (2008) and in academic research by Joanna Shepherd and Michael Kang.

Primary sources
  • John M. Olin Foundation, internal documents (available through Foundation archives): explicitly state the goal of changing law school intellectual culture to favor market reasoning.

e26958e6dd28790b.h:
UK, 1979–1990

Margaret Thatcher

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

'There is no such thing as society' — head of government, 1987; privatized state industries, broke unions, and exported the model globally

What they did

Thatcher's statement in a 1987 Woman's Own interview — "There is no such thing as society. There are individual men and women and there are families" — made the network's foundational assumption official state doctrine, spoken by a sitting head of government with global reach. Between 1979 and 1990, she privatized British Telecom, British Gas, British Airways, British Steel, British Rail, and water utilities; abolished exchange controls; deregulated the City of London (the "Big Bang," 1986); broke the trade unions (Miners' Strike, 1984); and cut the top income tax rate from 83% to 40%. She explicitly cited Hayek and the IEA as her intellectual foundations and carried a copy of Hayek's Constitution of Liberty in her handbag — which she famously slammed on a cabinet table, saying: "This is what we believe."

She understood herself as fighting a philosophical battle, not merely a policy one. Her statement to her policy team — "economics are the method; the object is to change the soul" — is the clearest articulation of what the entire network was doing: not adjusting tax rates but replacing the metaphysical framework through which people understand themselves and their obligations to each other.

Why — the gain and control

Thatcher's significance in this network is not merely as a policy implementer but as the person who made the metaphysical claim politically operational in a way that was immediately copied globally. The "Thatcher model" was explicitly exported to Eastern Europe after 1989 — Václav Klaus in Czechoslovakia and Leszek Balcerowicz in Poland both cited her as their template — and served as the political proof of concept that the IMF and World Bank pointed to when imposing structural adjustment programs on indebted nations across Africa, Latin America, and Asia. Her Chancellor Nigel Lawson's deregulation created conditions for the globalization of the network's financial framework. The IEA and Atlas Network used her government as the primary case study in their global replication strategy. Both primary sources are on record verbatim: "There is no such thing as society" (1987); "economics are the method; the object is to change the soul" (Sunday Times, 1981).

Primary sources
  • Margaret Thatcher, interview with Woman's Own, October 31, 1987: 'There is no such thing as society' — primary source.
  • Margaret Thatcher, interview with Sunday Times, May 3, 1981: 'Economics are the method; the object is to change the soul' — primary source.
  • Margaret Thatcher, The Downing Street Years (1993): her own account of the IEA's and Hayek's influence.
  • Hugo Young, One of Us (1989): the standard political biography, documenting her intellectual debts to the network.

623a81832e29e7fb.h:
Global, 1981–present

Atlas Network Global Franchise

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

The franchise mechanism: 500+ affiliated think tanks in 90+ countries, all replicating the same metaphysical framework — founded explicitly on Hayek's advice to Antony Fisher, with the IEA as the proof of concept and Atlas as the scaling operation

What they did

The Atlas Economic Research Foundation — now Atlas Network — was founded in 1981 by Antony Fisher, the same person who founded the IEA, explicitly to replicate the IEA model globally. It provides seed funding, training, and network connections to market-liberal think tanks worldwide. As of 2024, it connects over 500 affiliated think tanks in 90+ countries. Each affiliate operates independently, maintaining local legitimacy, but shares the same core framework: markets are moral arbiters, individual liberty is the supreme value, collective action is a threat to freedom, and profit is the measure of worth. The network has been documented providing strategic support to think tanks that campaign for specific deregulatory and privatization policies in countries that had previously maintained different frameworks.

The founding logic was Hayek's 1945 advice to Fisher — documented in Fisher's own writings — that changing the climate of opinion through "scholarly" institutes was more effective than direct political engagement. The IEA proved the concept in Britain. Atlas was built to replicate it in every country simultaneously.

Why — the gain and control

Atlas Network affiliates frame their mission as promoting "economic freedom" and "individual liberty" — not as spreading a particular metaphysics. The philosophical framework embedded in those terms (markets as neutral allocators, individual preferences as the legitimate unit of political life, collective action as a threat to freedom) is their shared premise, not their declared agenda. Whether this constitutes a coordinated ontological project or the organic spread of a worldview whose advocates genuinely believe in it is a distinction the documents themselves leave open; what is documented is the consistency of the premise across 500+ organizations and the funding network connecting them. Atlas Network affiliates have been documented intervening in specific policy debates at the national level across multiple countries. In Brazil, Atlas-affiliated think tanks were active in the policy environment preceding Bolsonaro's election and his government's deregulation program. In the UK, multiple Brexit-advocating think tanks had Atlas affiliations. In Latin America, Atlas-affiliated institutes produced the policy papers used to justify pension privatization, utility deregulation, and education reform across the region. The documented chain: Lee Fang's investigation in The Intercept (2017) traced Atlas's global network and funding sources; Dieter Plehwe's academic work documented the network's intellectual coherence and coordination mechanisms.

Primary sources
  • Antony Fisher, Must History Repeat Itself? (1974): Fisher's own account of the founding strategy and Hayek's advice.
  • Lee Fang, 'The Atlas Network: A Global Web of Think Tanks,' The Intercept (2017): documented Atlas's global operations and funding.
  • Dieter Plehwe and Bernhard Walpen, 'Between Network and Complex Organization: The Making of Neoliberal Knowledge and Hegemony' (2006): academic documentation of the network's coordination mechanisms.
  • Alexander Hertel-Fernandez, State Capture (2019): documented how Atlas-affiliated organizations shaped state-level legislation in the United States.

5ffaf65cb6b02015.h:
China, 1949–present

Chinese Communist Party

Government · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Implemented Soviet-style 'only matter is real' education for the world's largest population

What they did

The CCP adopted Soviet dialectical materialism through mandatory education, state media, and political culture for over a billion people. Traditional Chinese frameworks — Taoist, Confucian, and Buddhist cosmologies in which humans were embedded in living relationships with nature, ancestors, and cosmic order — were classified as feudal superstition and actively destroyed during the Cultural Revolution. Texts were burned. Practitioners were imprisoned or killed. The gap between what Chinese civilization had understood about self and world for three thousand years and what the CCP mandated was one of the largest deliberate metaphysical ruptures in human history.

Why — the gain and control

The CCP benefited from the same structural advantage all states gain from this framework: a population embedded in networks of communal obligation, ancestral relationship, and cosmic belonging is harder to direct than a population whose reality has been reduced to material and economic terms the state controls. The destruction of traditional Chinese ontology was simultaneously the destruction of its philosophical basis for collective resistance rooted in anything other than material interest.

Primary sources
  • Perry Link, The Uses of Literature (2000): documented how the CCP managed cultural production to enforce the materialist worldview.

Global TV & Hollywood Export Apparatus

Media / Distribution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

The US State Department and major studios treated film and television as deliberate instruments of ideological export — documented in official policy, studio correspondence, and Congressional testimony

What they did

77c580e71c0916a9.h:
Greece/Rome, 400 BCE–55 BCE

Democritus, Epicurus & Lucretius

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 400 BCE – 1620 CE · Ancient & Medieval Roots

First documented philosophical argument that reality consists entirely of atoms moving in void — no spirit, no purpose, no divine order

What they did

Democritus (~400 BCE) proposed that all of reality consists of indivisible particles (atoms) moving in void — nothing else exists. No spirit, no soul, no divine purpose — only matter and motion. Epicurus (~300 BCE) systematized this and founded a school that ran for 500 years. Lucretius (De Rerum Natura, ~55 BCE) transmitted it to Roman and later European culture in a form capable of being rediscovered. The text was lost after the 5th century CE and rediscovered in 1417 by Poggio Bracciolini in a German monastery — its reentry into European thought is documented by Stephen Greenblatt in The Swerve (2011).

Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French priest and scientist, deliberately revived Epicurean atomism and reconciled it with Christianity, making it available to the Royal Society generation. Newton's Opticks (1704) explicitly relied on Gassendi's atomism as its physical foundation.

Why — the gain and control

The atomist tradition mattered because it provided a complete, coherent alternative to the Aristotelian framework the Church endorsed — one with no room for soul, purpose, or divine governance of matter. When the Royal Society needed a physical framework independent of Church cosmology, Gassendi's revival of atomism was ready. Lucretius was the most dangerous book in the Church's view precisely because it made materialism beautiful, poetic, and complete. Its rediscovery and spread through the printing press was the underground infrastructure on which the Scientific Revolution's metaphysical claims rested.

One qualification matters here. The perceptual metaphysics of Democritus and Epicurus — the claim that reality consists entirely of atoms moving in void, with no soul, no purpose, no sacred relationships — is genuine, documented, and consequential. But the extraction-naturalizing function this visualization tracks was not operative in their time in any direct sense. Democritus and Lucretius were not legitimating colonial dispossession or industrial labor discipline; those institutions didn't exist. The connection is a long-fuse inheritance rather than a direct mechanism: their framework was dormant for a millennium, was revived deliberately by Gassendi specifically to serve the Royal Society's needs, and only then entered the chain of funded, institutionally promoted ideas that this visualization maps. The node belongs here because it supplied the raw material — the philosophical ground floor that says reality contains no living claims, no sacred relationships, nothing to belong to — that every subsequent node required and built upon. But the building happened elsewhere, by other hands, for other purposes.

Primary sources
  • Stephen Greenblatt, The Swerve: How the World Became Modern (2011): documented the rediscovery and transmission of Lucretius — Pulitzer Prize winner.
  • Catherine Wilson, Epicureanism at the Origins of Modernity (2008): documented Epicurean atomism's role in 17th-century natural philosophy.
  • Margaret Osler, Divine Will and the Mechanical Philosophy: Gassendi and Descartes (1994): documented Gassendi's deliberate revival of atomism as Royal Society infrastructure.
All connections

Holbach's Salon (inferred), La Mettrie & Mechanistic Materialism (inferred), Newton (inferred), Royal Society (inferred), Plato & The Academy (inferred), Axial Age State Religion (convergence)

bbbaa7f95981ea1f.h:
France/Prussia, 1747–1751

La Mettrie & Mechanistic Materialism

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

First systematic published argument that humans are purely material machines — written by a military surgeon, banned in France, protected by Frederick the Great

What they did

Julien Offray de La Mettrie published L'Homme Machine (Man a Machine) in 1747 anonymously in Leiden. His argument: the soul does not exist. Humans are biological machines, more complex than other animals but different only in degree. Thought is what the brain does, exactly as digestion is what the stomach does. Moral and emotional life are mechanical processes. He was expelled from France, then from the Netherlands. Frederick the Great gave him refuge and a position at the Berlin Academy of Sciences — where he died in 1751, having made the complete materialist case about human beings in published, popular form for the first time. Frederick wrote his eulogy personally.

Why — the gain and control

La Mettrie's significance in this network is that he made the claim explicitly and completely for the first time in a form that circulated — before Holbach, before Büchner, before Darwin. The institutional structure matters: he was protected by a major European state (Prussia) precisely because Frederick the Great needed intellectuals who could legitimate secular governance against Church authority. Materialism about human nature was useful to states as well as merchants: it dissolved the theological basis for Church governance of family, sexuality, and conscience. Frederick's patronage was documented in correspondence and is available in Frederick's collected writings.

Primary sources
  • Julien de La Mettrie, L'Homme Machine (1747): primary source — the first complete published argument that humans are purely material machines.
  • Ann Thomson, Bodies of Thought: Science, Religion, and the Soul in the Early Enlightenment (2008): documented La Mettrie's work and Prussian patronage.
  • Frederick the Great, eulogy for La Mettrie (1751): primary source — the king's personal defense of a materialist philosopher — in Frederick's collected correspondence.

bf67ac7454ca5afa.h:
USA/UK, 1920–present

Biological Determinism & Pioneer Fund

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Pioneer Fund (1937) paid researchers to produce evidence for hereditary racial hierarchy — Arthur Jensen, Herrnstein & Murray — the same claim as eugenics dressed as psychology

What they did

Cyril Burt (1883–1971) produced the most influential IQ twin studies of the 20th century, demonstrating strong heritability of intelligence. His data was found fraudulent after his death (Leon Kamin, 1974). Arthur Jensen's "How Much Can We Boost IQ and Scholastic Achievement?" (Harvard Educational Review, 1969) argued that the 15-point IQ gap between Black and white Americans was largely hereditary and not addressable by education — and was funded by the Pioneer Fund. The Pioneer Fund (founded 1937 by Harry Laughlin, the author of the US model sterilization law, and Wickliffe Draper) explicitly funded research demonstrating racial hierarchy in intelligence. Its grants supported Jensen, Richard Lynn, J. Philippe Rushton, and eventually the research infrastructure behind Charles Murray and Richard Herrnstein's The Bell Curve (1994).

Pioneer Fund grants are public record. The Bell Curve's acknowledgments cite Pioneer Fund-supported researchers as primary sources for its claims about race and intelligence.

Why — the gain and control

The Pioneer Fund is a documented funding apparatus with an explicitly stated eugenicist founding mission — Wickliffe Draper's correspondence, available in archives, states the goal of demonstrating racial hierarchy in intelligence as scientific fact. The fund operated continuously from 1937 through the Bell Curve era and beyond. The ontological claim is identical to classical eugenics: human beings differ in biological worth, and these differences are hereditary and immutable. The policy implication — that investing in certain populations is biologically futile — was the argument's payload. The Bell Curve was published by The Free Press (Simon & Schuster) and received major coverage. Its policy influence on welfare reform discussions is documented.

Primary sources
  • William H. Tucker, The Funding of Scientific Racism: Wickliffe Draper and the Pioneer Fund (2002): documented the Pioneer Fund's founding mission and grant history — primary documentary account.
  • Leon Kamin, The Science and Politics of IQ (1974): documented Burt's data fraud.
  • Richard Herrnstein and Charles Murray, The Bell Curve (1994): the text acknowledges Pioneer Fund researchers — primary source on the funding chain.
  • Stephen Jay Gould, The Mismeasure of Man (1981, expanded 1996): standard critical account of biological determinism's institutional history.

8440b9bbb74a07f7.h:
Germany, 1844

Max Stirner

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1750–1870 · Science Goes Public

All social obligations — state, law, morality, God — are 'spooks': illusions. The individual self is the only reality. Direct influence on Nietzsche, Bakunin, and Rand.

What they did

Max Stirner (Johann Kaspar Schmidt) published The Ego and Its Own (Der Einzige und sein Eigentum) in 1844. His argument: every concept that claims authority over the individual — God, state, law, morality, nation, even "humanity" — is a Spook, a mental ghost with no real existence. The individual self is the only real entity. Every claim on the individual that cannot be grounded in the individual's own interest and power is fraud. He worked as a schoolteacher in Berlin and died in poverty in 1856. His book was suppressed but circulated widely in radical circles — Marx and Engels spent 300 pages of The German Ideology (1845) refuting him, which is the primary evidence of his impact on the left.

Why — the gain and control

Stirner's significance in this network is his influence on subsequent actors who had institutional reach: Nietzsche read him (though denied it — denied by Nietzsche but documented by scholars); Bakunin's anarchism drew on him; Emma Goldman cited him; Ayn Rand's Objectivism is essentially Stirner with a capitalist economics attached. His specific move — declaring all social obligation to be illusion — is the philosophical position that the rest of the network's output delivers to mass audiences without attribution. The Rand node in this visualization is his most institutionalized successor.

Primary sources
  • Max Stirner, The Ego and Its Own (1844/tr. Byington 1907): primary source.
  • Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The German Ideology (1845, published 1932): 300-page refutation — primary evidence of impact.
  • R.W.K. Paterson, The Nihilistic Egoist: Max Stirner (1971): standard intellectual account documenting influence on Nietzsche, Bakunin, and anarchist tradition.

e68fe6bcc359e29f.h:
Germany/Switzerland, 1882–1889

Friedrich Nietzsche

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

'God is dead' — diagnosed the collapse of the moral foundations of Western civilization and predicted nihilism as its consequence; his work was then systematically distorted by his sister and by Social Darwinists

What they did

Nietzsche's three most consequential texts: The Gay Science (1882) — "God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him" — diagnosed the collapse of the transcendent grounding of Western morality; Beyond Good and Evil (1886) — a systematic critique of the philosophical assumptions of both Christian and Kantian ethics; On the Genealogy of Morality (1887) — a historical argument that moral systems are instruments of power rather than transcendent truths. He held the Chair of Classical Philology at Basel from 1869 and resigned due to illness in 1879.

Nietzsche did not endorse nihilism — he diagnosed it as the cultural crisis that follows the death of God, and considered it a problem to be overcome. His sister Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche controlled his archive after his mental collapse in 1889, selectively published his notes as The Will to Power (1901), and deliberately associated his work with German nationalism and later with Nazi ideology. This distortion is documented by Walter Kaufmann (Nietzsche, 1950) and is the primary scholarly consensus.

Why — the gain and control

The mechanism of Nietzsche's effect in this network was his distortion rather than his actual argument. The phrase "God is dead" was detached from its context of crisis and mourning and broadcast as liberation. "Will to power" was detached from its psychological meaning and deployed as justification for domination. His sister's deliberate archive manipulation turned his work into a text available for fascist and Social Darwinist deployment. The original thinker and the deployed weapon were two different things — a distinction the popular audience of Spencer, Haeckel, and later the science bestsellers never encountered.

Primary sources
  • Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science (1882), Beyond Good and Evil (1886), On the Genealogy of Morality (1887): primary sources.
  • Walter Kaufmann, Nietzsche: Philosopher, Psychologist, Antichrist (1950): documented the distortion by his sister and the recovery of the original text.
  • Ben Macintyre, Forgotten Fatherland: The Search for Elisabeth Nietzsche (1992): documented Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's deliberate manipulation of the archive.

Error Theory & Analytic Metaethics

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

J.L. Mackie's Error Theory argued moral statements are systematically false — no moral facts exist — and this became the mainstream position in analytic philosophy departments globally

What they did

J.L. Mackie's Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong (1977), written at University College Oxford, argued that all moral statements make a claim (that objective moral facts exist) that is necessarily false, because the world contains no objective prescriptive properties. This position — error theory — became one of the three main positions in analytic metaethics, taught in philosophy courses globally. Its mainstream alternatives (non-cognitivism, expressivism) also deny objective moral facts, just on different grounds. The version of moral philosophy taught in most university courses from the 1980s onward operates within a framework in which no moral statement can be objectively true — the disagreement is about what kind of non-truth moral statements are.

Oxford, Harvard, Princeton, and their global satellites then exported this framework through the Commonwealth and American university systems to the same populations receiving the rest of the network's outputs.

Why — the gain and control

The significance of error theory in this network is not that Mackie intended his work as ideological. He was doing rigorous analytic philosophy. But the combination of error theory (no moral facts exist) with the broader materialist framework (humans are physical beings in a physical world) produces a population for whom both metaphysical and moral foundations are eliminated simultaneously. A person who has absorbed Churchland's eliminative materialism and Mackie's error theory has, in their educational formation, no philosophical basis for asserting that either their experience or their moral claims refer to anything beyond their own neurochemistry. This is the logical completion of the network's project — and it was delivered through university philosophy courses as established academic consensus.

Cosmic Nihilism & Scientific Pessimism

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

Bertrand Russell, Steven Weinberg, and Carl Sagan gave cosmic indifference scientific credibility — delivered through the popular science and academic prestige networks

What they did

Three figures in distinct phases: Bertrand Russell's "A Free Man's Worship" (1903) — "brief and powerless is Man's life; on him and all his race the slow, sure doom falls pitiless and dark. Blind to good and evil, reckless of destruction, omnipotent matter rolls on its relentless way." Russell was at Cambridge; this essay was widely anthologized. Steven Weinberg's The First Three Minutes (1977, Nobel Prize in Physics 1979) closed with: "The more the universe seems comprehensible, the more it also seems pointless." This was cited in thousands of subsequent documents.

Russell and Weinberg were making explicit claims about meaninglessness. A third figure frequently cited alongside them — Carl Sagan's Pale Blue Dot (1994) — is different in kind: Sagan used cosmic smallness to argue for humility and ecological care, not nihilism. He explicitly called for protecting the Earth because of our vulnerability. His inclusion alongside Russell and Weinberg is a documented misreading in the literature — the same "tiny speck" image was deployed by nihilists who did not read Sagan's actual argument. That misreading is itself a mechanism worth noting: the cosmic-smallness image circulated independently of its author's intent, available for appropriation into a framework Sagan explicitly opposed.

These statements by Russell and Weinberg were not side products of their careers — they were deliberately composed public philosophical statements by scientists of major institutional prestige, using that prestige to lend the authority of physics to the claim that the cosmos carries no meaning.

Why — the gain and control

The mechanism here is scientific prestige deployed for metaphysical statement. Russell, Weinberg, and Sagan were not making scientific claims when they described the universe as pointless or humanity as insignificant — they were making philosophical claims using the authority their scientific work gave them. Weinberg's statement in particular has been cited by philosophers and scientists across multiple disciplines as if it were a scientific finding. The combination of cosmic nihilism (universe is indifferent and purposeless) with eliminative materialism (consciousness is a brain process) and error theory (no moral facts exist) delivers a complete metaphysical picture to the educated public through the prestige networks of Nobel Prize winners and flagship popular science.

Primary sources
  • Bertrand Russell, 'A Free Man's Worship' (1903): primary source — widely anthologized philosophical statement of cosmic nihilism.
  • Steven Weinberg, The First Three Minutes (1977): primary source — 'the more the universe seems comprehensible, the more it also seems pointless.'
  • Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space (1994): primary source — the Pale Blue Dot meditation on human insignificance.

USA/UK, 1975–2000

Sociobiology & Ultra-Darwinism

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

E.O. Wilson's 'Sociobiology' (1975) and Dawkins's 'The Selfish Gene' (1976) argued all human behavior is determined by evolutionary pressures on gene replication — NSF and Harvard funded

What they did

E.O. Wilson's Sociobiology: The New Synthesis (1975), written at Harvard and supported by NSF grants, argued that all social behavior — including human ethics, religion, altruism, aggression, and sexuality — can be fully explained by evolutionary pressures on gene replication. He extended this to humans explicitly in On Human Nature (1978). Richard Dawkins's The Selfish Gene (1976) provided the gene-centered framework: organisms, including humans, are "survival machines" built by genes to propagate themselves; love, cooperation, and apparent altruism are gene propagation strategies.

The controversy was documented and extensive: the Sociobiology Study Group (Richard Lewontin, Stephen Jay Gould, and 13 others) published a detailed critique in The New York Review of Books (1975), arguing the framework naturalized existing social hierarchies. Wilson had water poured on his head at an AAAS meeting in 1978. The controversy itself massively amplified the framework's reach.

Why — the gain and control

The NSF funding chain is documented: Wilson's research at Harvard's Museum of Comparative Zoology was federally funded through standard scientific grants. The ontological claim deployed through this apparatus: every human capacity — moral feeling, religious impulse, communal solidarity — is a gene propagation strategy that natural selection shaped because it improved reproductive fitness. This claim, given the scientific authority of Harvard and NSF funding, reached popular audiences through Dawkins's books (already in the sci_bestsellers node) and through every introductory psychology course that adopted evolutionary psychology as its framework. The implication — that altruism is self-deception about one's genes' interests — is the philosophical conclusion the Chicago School's economic framework arrived at through a different route.

Primary sources
  • E.O. Wilson, Sociobiology: The New Synthesis (1975) and On Human Nature (1978): primary sources — Harvard, NSF funded.
  • Ullica Segerstrale, Defenders of the Truth: The Battle for Science in the Sociobiology Debate (2000): documented the controversy and the institutional stakes.
  • Richard Lewontin et al., 'Against Sociobiology,' New York Review of Books, November 13, 1975: primary critique — documented in real time.

6053fc5142d14dd5.h:
UK/USA/Germany, 1883–1945

Eugenics Record Office & Galton Network

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Francis Galton coined 'eugenics' (1883); Carnegie and Harriman funded the Eugenics Record Office (1910); Rockefeller funded Nazi eugenics programs — the same industrial fortunes as the Chicago School

What they did

Francis Galton, Darwin's cousin, coined eugenics in 1883 and established the Galton Laboratory at University College London (funded by his estate). Charles Davenport used this framework to found the Eugenics Record Office (ERO) at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, in 1910 — funded by the Carnegie Institution (verified in Carnegie annual reports) and by Mary Harriman (the railroad fortune), documented by Edwin Black in War Against the Weak (2003). The ERO collected family histories from across the US, produced model sterilization laws adopted in 30 states, and provided expert testimony in Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court case upholding compulsory sterilization ("three generations of imbeciles are enough" — Oliver Wendell Holmes).

The Rockefeller Foundation funded the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology, Human Heredity and Eugenics in Berlin from 1927 — documented in its own grant records and in Stefan Kühl's The Nazi Connection (1994). In 1927, the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute was a mainstream scientific institution in the Weimar Republic; the Rockefeller Foundation's funding reflected the era's widespread acceptance of hereditary research across the scientific community. Funding continued after Hitler's rise in 1933, and the Foundation's archives show internal debate about whether to continue (documented in Paul Weindling, Health, Race and German Politics, 1989). The Foundation eventually wound down its grants to the Institute in the late 1930s. The post-1933 continuation is the more troubling documented fact; the pre-1933 funding requires the context of what the institution appeared to be at the time. The relationship between the ERO's model sterilization law and the Nazi Racial Hygiene Laws (1935) is documented but requires precision: Nazi legal architects cited American sterilization laws as precedent during Nuremberg testimony, and some provisions show direct influence. However, the Nazi laws were more extreme than their American analogs, drew significantly on German eugenic traditions that developed independently of American models, and went far beyond the ERO's scope. The influence was real and acknowledged; calling them "explicitly modeled on" American law overstates the causal relationship (Stefan Kühl, The Nazi Connection, 1994, is careful on this point).

Why — the gain and control

The funding overlap with existing network nodes is documented and specific: the Carnegie Institution funded both the ERO and the early University of Chicago (which became the Chicago School's base). The Rockefeller Foundation funded both the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for eugenics and the social science research that fed into the Chicago School's economic assumptions. These were not different factions of capital — they were the same foundations, making grants that reflected the same underlying ontological commitment: humans are natural objects, biological quality varies between individuals and groups, some should not reproduce, and the role of science is to manage this variation for the good of the species. The ontological claim was the competitive-individual framework pushed to its biological conclusion.

Primary sources
  • Edwin Black, War Against the Weak: Eugenics and America's Campaign to Create a Master Race (2003): primary documentary account — Carnegie and Harriman funding documented from institutional archives.
  • Stefan Kühl, The Nazi Connection: Eugenics, American Racism, and German National Socialism (1994): documented Rockefeller Foundation funding of Kaiser Wilhelm Institute.
  • Daniel Kevles, In the Name of Eugenics (1985): standard history of the Anglo-American eugenics movement.
  • Paul Lombardo, Three Generations, No Imbeciles: Eugenics, the Supreme Court, and Buck v. Bell (2008): documented ERO role in Buck v. Bell.

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1859–1910 · Evolution as Total Worldview

Francis Galton coined 'eugenics' (1883); Carnegie and Harriman funded the Eugenics Record Office (1910); Rockefeller funded Nazi eugenics programs — the same industrial fortunes as the Chicago School

What they did

Francis Galton, Darwin's cousin, coined eugenics in 1883 and established the Galton Laboratory at University College London (funded by his estate). Charles Davenport used this framework to found the Eugenics Record Office (ERO) at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, in 1910 — funded by the Carnegie Institution (verified in Carnegie annual reports) and by Mary Harriman (the railroad fortune), documented by Edwin Black in War Against the Weak (2003). The ERO collected family histories from across the US, produced model sterilization laws adopted in 30 states, and provided expert testimony in Buck v. Bell (1927), the Supreme Court case upholding compulsory sterilization ("three generations of imbeciles are enough" — Oliver Wendell Holmes).

The Rockefeller Foundation funded the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Anthropology, Human Heredity and Eugenics in Berlin from 1927 — documented in its own grant records and in Stefan Kühl's The Nazi Connection (1994). In 1927, the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute was a mainstream scientific institution in the Weimar Republic; the Rockefeller Foundation's funding reflected the era's widespread acceptance of hereditary research across the scientific community. Funding continued after Hitler's rise in 1933, and the Foundation's archives show internal debate about whether to continue (documented in Paul Weindling, Health, Race and German Politics, 1989). The Foundation eventually wound down its grants to the Institute in the late 1930s. The post-1933 continuation is the more troubling documented fact; the pre-1933 funding requires the context of what the institution appeared to be at the time. The relationship between the ERO's model sterilization law and the Nazi Racial Hygiene Laws (1935) is documented but requires precision: Nazi legal architects cited American sterilization laws as precedent during Nuremberg testimony, and some provisions show direct influence. However, the Nazi laws were more extreme than their American analogs, drew significantly on German eugenic traditions that developed independently of American models, and went far beyond the ERO's scope. The influence was real and acknowledged; calling them "explicitly modeled on" American law overstates the causal relationship (Stefan Kühl, The Nazi Connection, 1994, is careful on this point).

Why — the gain and control

The funding overlap with existing network nodes is documented and specific: the Carnegie Institution funded both the ERO and the early University of Chicago (which became the Chicago School's base). The Rockefeller Foundation funded both the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for eugenics and the social science research that fed into the Chicago School's economic assumptions. These were not different factions of capital — they were the same foundations, making grants that reflected the same underlying ontological commitment: humans are natural objects, biological quality varies between individuals and groups, some should not reproduce, and the role of science is to manage this variation for the good of the species. The ontological claim was the competitive-individual framework pushed to its biological conclusion.

Primary sources
  • Edwin Black, War Against the Weak: Eugenics and America's Campaign to Create a Master Race (2003): primary documentary account — Carnegie and Harriman funding documented from institutional archives.
  • Stefan Kühl, The Nazi Connection: Eugenics, American Racism, and German National Socialism (1994): documented Rockefeller Foundation funding of Kaiser Wilhelm Institute.
  • Daniel Kevles, In the Name of Eugenics (1985): standard history of the Anglo-American eugenics movement.
  • Paul Lombardo, Three Generations, No Imbeciles: Eugenics, the Supreme Court, and Buck v. Bell (2008): documented ERO role in Buck v. Bell.

USA/Global, 1913–1980

Behaviorism & Institutional Deployment

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1910–1960 · Academic Lock-In

Watson and Skinner argued the mind is irrelevant — only measurable behavior matters — and this was institutionalized in US schools, prisons, corporate HR, and advertising with documented funding

What they did

John Watson's "Psychology as the Behaviorist Views It" (1913) declared the complete rejection of consciousness, introspection, and inner life as scientific concepts. Only observable, measurable behavior counts. B.F. Skinner extended this into a total account of human life: Science and Human Behavior (1953), Verbal Behavior (1957), Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971). His argument: freedom and dignity are pre-scientific concepts that must be abandoned for a science of behavior — operant conditioning — which controls behavior through reinforcement schedules.

The institutional deployment was documented and extensive: the Office of Naval Research funded Skinner's pigeon guidance research from 1943. The US Department of Defense funded behavioral modification programs. The controversial "CASE" (Contingencies Applicable to Special Education) and prison behavioral modification programs of the 1960s–70s were federally and state funded. Corporate HR departments adopted Skinner's reinforcement schedule framework for incentive design — documented in Frederick Herzberg's parallel research and in Alfie Kohn's Punished by Rewards (1993).

Why — the gain and control

Behaviorism's institutional significance is that it provided a complete framework for human management that explicitly deleted the inner life. If humans are input-output systems — stimulus-response machines — then management is engineering: arrange the reinforcement schedule correctly and the behavior follows. This framework was adopted by education systems (standardized testing as reinforcement), prison management (token economies), advertising (conditioning consumer response), and corporate HR (performance management systems). All of these are documented. The ontological claim — that what happens inside a person is irrelevant to their management — is the Royal Society's "only what can be measured is real" applied to organizational control of human beings.

Primary sources
  • B.F. Skinner, Beyond Freedom and Dignity (1971): primary source — explicit statement that freedom and dignity are pre-scientific concepts.
  • Alfie Kohn, Punished by Rewards: The Trouble with Gold Stars, Incentive Plans, A's, Praise, and Other Bribes (1993): documented corporate and educational deployment of behaviorist reinforcement.
  • James McConnell, behavioral modification programs in US prisons (1970s): documented in debates in Psychology Today and congressional hearings.
  • Office of Naval Research: Skinner's pigeon project contract, 1943 — primary source on federal funding of behavioral research.

9409c25088e6fde5.h:
USA/Global, 1980–present

Biological Psychiatry & Pharmaceutical DSM

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

The DSM-III (1980) reclassified mental distress as biological dysfunction — pharmaceutical companies funded the working groups and medical school departments that defined the diagnostic categories

What they did

The DSM-III (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual, Third Edition, 1980), led by Robert Spitzer at Columbia, explicitly abandoned psychodynamic frameworks and reclassified mental disorders as biological dysfunctions defined by symptom checklists. This was not a scientific finding — it was a deliberate theoretical reorientation. The manual did not specify biological causes because none had been established; it specified behavioral symptoms. The framing was explicitly biological — subsequent pharmaceutical marketing would popularize the chemical imbalance theory as the explanation — though this specific claim was contested within psychiatry (the APA itself never formally endorsed a single neurochemical model, and by the 2010s NIMH moved toward its RDoC framework for different theoretical reasons). The practical framing delivered to patients and public was that mental distress is a medical condition caused by neurochemical dysfunction, not by circumstances, relationships, or meaning.

The pharmaceutical industry had direct material interest in this reclassification: a biological model of mental illness requires biological treatment (drugs), not psychotherapy or social intervention. Documented pharmaceutical funding of DSM working groups is in: David Healy, The Antidepressant Era (1997); Robert Whitaker, Anatomy of an Epidemic (2010); and Marcia Angell (former editor, New England Journal of Medicine), "The Illusions of Psychiatry" (New York Review of Books, 2011). The "chemical imbalance" theory (serotonin deficit = depression) was never validated and was disavowed by its original proponents — this is documented in Joanna Moncrieff's research.

Why — the gain and control

The ontological claim is distinct from anything in the existing visualization: human mental distress is a biological malfunction, not a response to circumstances, relationships, meaninglessness, or alienation. The appropriate response is biochemical, not relational, social, or existential. This claim, delivered by the most authoritative medical institution in the world (American Psychiatric Association) and backed by pharmaceutical marketing budgets that dwarfed any think tank, reached a larger population more quickly than any previous node in this network. Its practical effect: the redirection of help-seeking from community, relationship, and meaning toward pharmacology — regardless of whether the neurochemical model was correct.

The entry's claims require careful framing. Biological factors in mental illness are documented: genetic studies show heritable components in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder; brain imaging identifies structural correlates of some conditions; neurotransmitter systems are involved in mood regulation. The biological psychiatry framework is not simply a pharmaceutical invention — it reflects real evidence and has produced treatments that work for many patients.

The documented controversy is narrower. The specific serotonin-deficiency theory of depression — promoted heavily in pharmaceutical marketing and patient education from the 1990s onward — was never established as the primary mechanism, and the 2022 Moncrieff et al. umbrella review found no consistent evidence for it. Whether it accurately describes the mechanism or not, SSRIs produce measurable effects in clinical trials; the causal story behind those effects is genuinely contested. That distinction — between the marketing narrative and the underlying science — is what the critical literature (Moncrieff, Healy, Angell) documents.

The DSM claim also requires precision: DSM working groups included members with pharmaceutical ties, but many did not, and the process involved extensive clinical input from practicing psychiatrists, researchers, and patient advocates. That the categories developed under conditions of pharmaceutical influence is documented; that they were primarily driven by that influence overstates a complex institutional process. The more defensible claim: the diagnostic framing that emerged — behavioral symptom checklists without specified causes — was deployed by pharmaceutical marketing to support disease-model narratives the underlying manual did not actually assert. The gap between what the DSM said and what patients were told is documentable; the causal role of pharma in that gap is documented but contested in its extent.

Primary sources
  • Robert Whitaker, Anatomy of an Epidemic: Magic Bullets, Psychiatric Drugs, and the Astonishing Rise of Mental Illness in America (2010): documented pharmaceutical funding and the failure of the chemical imbalance theory.
  • David Healy, The Antidepressant Era (1997): documented pharmaceutical industry's role in shaping DSM diagnostic categories.
  • Marcia Angell, 'The Illusions of Psychiatry,' New York Review of Books, July 14, 2011: former NEJM editor's account of pharmaceutical influence on psychiatric diagnosis.
  • Irving Kirsch, The Emperor's New Drugs: Exploding the Antidepressant Myth (2010): documented the failure of the biological model in clinical trials.
All connections

The biological psychiatry framework is not simply a pharmaceutical invention — it reflects real evidence and has produced treatments that work for many patients.

The documented controversy is narrower. The specific serotonin-deficiency theory of depression — promoted heavily in pharmaceutical marketing and patient education from the 1990s onward — was never established as the primary mechanism, and the 2022 Moncrieff et al. umbrella review found no consistent evidence for it. Whether it accurately describes the mechanism or not, SSRIs produce measurable effects in clinical trials; the causal story behind those effects is genuinely contested. That distinction — between the marketing narrative and the underlying science — is what the critical literature (Moncrieff, Healy, Angell) documents.

The DSM claim also requires precision: DSM working groups included members with pharmaceutical ties, but many did not, and the process involved extensive clinical input from practicing psychiatrists, researchers, and patient advocates. That the categories developed under conditions of pharmaceutical influence is documented; that they were primarily driven by that influence overstates a complex institutional process. The more defensible claim: the diagnostic framing that emerged — behavioral symptom checklists without specified causes — was deployed by pharmaceutical marketing to support disease-model narratives the underlying manual did not actually assert. The gap between what the DSM said and what patients were told is documentable; the causal role of pharma in that gap is documented but contested in its extent.

Primary sources
  • Robert Whitaker, Anatomy of an Epidemic: Magic Bullets, Psychiatric Drugs, and the Astonishing Rise of Mental Illness in America (2010): documented pharmaceutical funding and the failure of the chemical imbalance theory.
  • David Healy, The Antidepressant Era (1997): documented pharmaceutical industry's role in shaping DSM diagnostic categories.
  • Marcia Angell, 'The Illusions of Psychiatry,' New York Review of Books, July 14, 2011: former NEJM editor's account of pharmaceutical influence on psychiatric diagnosis.
  • Irving Kirsch, The Emperor's New Drugs: Exploding the Antidepressant Myth (2010): documented the failure of the biological model in clinical trials.

MBA & Management Consulting Pipeline

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

Harvard Business School + McKinsey + Friedman's shareholder primacy: the pipeline that trained every person running a corporation, hospital, school, and government department to treat efficiency as the only value

What they did

Three interlocking components: Harvard Business School (founded 1908 with endowments from industrial capital — the same class as Carnegie and Rockefeller) adopted Frederick Winslow Taylor's scientific management as foundational: organizations are machines, workers are interchangeable parts, efficiency is the only metric. Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management (1911) proposed time-and-motion studies to optimize every physical movement of factory workers — documented in Robert Kanigel, The One Best Way (1997).

Friedman's Shareholder Primacy (1970 NYT essay: "The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits") was adopted as HBS curriculum and became the Business Roundtable's official doctrine 1997–2019 — when it was formally reversed in a 2019 statement (documented). It reshaped corporate governance globally by defining the corporation as a mechanism for returning value to shareholders and treating any other purpose as a misuse of resources.

McKinsey & Company extended this framework to every sector: governments, healthcare, education, nonprofits, military. Duff McDonald's The Firm (2013) documented McKinsey's explicit mandate to spread the efficiency-as-only-value framework globally. McKinsey's work for the UK NHS (privatization design), the US Defense Department (base closures), the IMF (structural adjustment program design) is documented.

Why — the gain and control

Peter Drucker coined "human resources" in The Practice of Management (1954) — documented in Andrea Gabor, The Capitalist Philosophers (2000). The phrase is the ontological claim in two words: people in organizations are a resource equivalent to capital and material resources, to be deployed and managed for organizational output. Every manager trained in an MBA program and every organization that hired a McKinsey consultant after 1960 received this framework as management science. It reached organizations the Chicago School's economic theory never directly touched — hospitals, schools, government departments, charities — and told each of them that efficiency (measurable output per unit input) was the only legitimate metric for their activities. The Royal Society's declaration that only what can be measured is real, applied to every human organization.

  • Milton Friedman, 'The Social Responsibility of Business is to Increase its Profits,' New York Times Magazine, September 13, 1970: primary source.
  • Business Roundtable, 'Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation' (2019): primary source — explicit reversal of the Friedman doctrine after 22 years.
  • Duff McDonald, The Firm: The Story of McKinsey and Its Secret Influence on American Business (2013): documented McKinsey's global deployment of the efficiency framework.
  • Lynn Stout, The Shareholder Value Myth (2012): documented how shareholder primacy doctrine reshaped corporate governance globally.

003924f5381cdbcb.h:

Sartre & French Existentialism

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

'Existence precedes essence' — humans have no fixed nature; Les Temps Modernes delivered this to the postwar global educated audience through a dedicated journal and Gallimard's publishing apparatus

What they did

Jean-Paul Sartre's Being and Nothingness (1943) and "Existentialism is a Humanism" (1946 lecture, 500 attendees, published immediately by Nagel) made the claim: existence precedes essence — humans have no given nature, no fixed soul, no predetermined meaning. We are "condemned to be free," thrown into a universe without inherent purpose, and responsible entirely for what we make of ourselves. Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) applied the same framework to gender.

The institutional apparatus was distinct and substantial: Les Temps Modernes (journal, 1945–2018), edited by Sartre with Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty, published political and philosophical essays to a readership across France, Europe, and the decolonizing world. Gallimard (the publisher) distributed globally. Sartre's UNESCO connections and his refusal of the Nobel Prize in 1964 — explained as a refusal to allow his work to be institutionalized — itself became a global media event that amplified his framework. By the 1960s, existentialism was the dominant philosophical vocabulary of the educated young in Europe, Latin America, North Africa, and East Asia.

Why — the gain and control

The relationship between Sartre's framework and the network's project requires care. Sartre himself was explicitly and consistently anti-capitalist, anti-colonial, and opposed to the economic interests this network served — he supported independence movements across Africa and Asia, signed the Manifesto of the 121 against the Algerian War, and aligned with Marxist critique of capital throughout his career. He did not serve the network's interests and did not intend to.

The argument here is narrower and more honest: existence precedes essence — the claim that humans have no fixed nature, no inherent connections, and are entirely self-creating — is structurally convergent with the isolated-individual framework the network needed, regardless of the political direction Sartre pointed it. This is philosophical affinity across opposing political projects, not historical causation. The same metaphysical ground floor — no given human nature, no inherent communal belonging — supports both Sartre's revolutionary subject and the network's consuming individual. Which is not a claim that Sartre caused the latter or intended it, but that the philosophical materials were available to both, and the network's apparatus was better resourced to disseminate one use of them than the other.

What can be documented is the institutional reception — Sartre's ideas reached mass audiences in the same decade and through some of the same publishing and media networks as the science bestsellers and New Atheism. What cannot be documented is a transmission mechanism from his metaphysics to consumer individualism that doesn't run through the network's own apparatus appropriating his vocabulary for different ends.

Primary sources
  • Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943) and 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946): primary sources.
  • Annie Cohen-Solal, Sartre: A Life (1987): documented the institutional apparatus — Les Temps Modernes, Gallimard, UNESCO connections.
  • Michael Kelly, Modern French Marxism (1982): documented existentialism's spread through French publishing and its global reach.
All connections

Friedrich Nietzsche (documented), Error Theory & Analytic Metaethics (inferred)

Paris, 1945–1980

Sartre & French Existentialism

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

'Existence precedes essence' — humans have no fixed nature; Les Temps Modernes delivered this to the postwar global educated audience through a dedicated journal and Gallimard's publishing apparatus

What they did

Jean-Paul Sartre's Being and Nothingness (1943) and "Existentialism is a Humanism" (1946 lecture, 500 attendees, published immediately by Nagel) made the claim: existence precedes essence — humans have no given nature, no fixed soul, no predetermined meaning. We are "condemned to be free," thrown into a universe without inherent purpose, and responsible entirely for what we make of ourselves. Simone de Beauvoir's The Second Sex (1949) applied the same framework to gender.

The institutional apparatus was distinct and substantial: Les Temps Modernes (journal, 1945–2018), edited by Sartre with Beauvoir and Merleau-Ponty, published political and philosophical essays to a readership across France, Europe, and the decolonizing world. Gallimard (the publisher) distributed globally. Sartre's UNESCO connections and his refusal of the Nobel Prize in 1964 — explained as a refusal to allow his work to be institutionalized — itself became a global media event that amplified his framework. By the 1960s, existentialism was the dominant philosophical vocabulary of the educated young in Europe, Latin America, North Africa, and East Asia.

Why — the gain and control

The relationship between Sartre's framework and the network's project requires care. Sartre himself was explicitly and consistently anti-capitalist, anti-colonial, and opposed to the economic interests this network served — he supported independence movements across Africa and Asia, signed the Manifesto of the 121 against the Algerian War, and aligned with Marxist critique of capital throughout his career. He did not serve the network's interests and did not intend to.

The argument here is narrower and more honest: existence precedes essence — the claim that humans have no fixed nature, no inherent connections, and are entirely self-creating — is structurally convergent with the isolated-individual framework the network needed, regardless of the political direction Sartre pointed it. This is philosophical affinity across opposing political projects, not historical causation. The same metaphysical ground floor — no given human nature, no inherent communal belonging — supports both Sartre's revolutionary subject and the network's consuming individual. Which is not a claim that Sartre caused the latter or intended it, but that the philosophical materials were available to both, and the network's apparatus was better resourced to disseminate one use of them than the other.

What can be documented is the institutional reception — Sartre's ideas reached mass audiences in the same decade and through some of the same publishing and media networks as the science bestsellers and New Atheism. What cannot be documented is a transmission mechanism from his metaphysics to consumer individualism that doesn't run through the network's own apparatus appropriating his vocabulary for different ends.

Primary sources
  • Jean-Paul Sartre, Being and Nothingness (1943) and 'Existentialism is a Humanism' (1946): primary sources.
  • Annie Cohen-Solal, Sartre: A Life (1987): documented the institutional apparatus — Les Temps Modernes, Gallimard, UNESCO connections.
  • Michael Kelly, Modern French Marxism (1982): documented existentialism's spread through French publishing and its global reach.

8819133e70cacc31.h:
USA/Global, 1956–present

Cognitive Science & Computational Mind

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1945–1990 · Cold War & Global Export

Turing, Marr, Chomsky — NSF and DARPA funded the claim that cognition IS computation, mind is software, and a complete computational description replaces explanation of experience

What they did

Three foundational moves: Alan Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence" (1950) proposed that if a machine could not be distinguished from a human in conversation, there was no meaningful sense in which the machine did not think — the Turing Test reframed the question of mind as a question of behavioral output rather than inner experience. Noam Chomsky's Syntactic Structures (1957) proposed that language is governed by innate computational rules, not learned through behavioral conditioning — replacing Skinner's stimulus-response with an internal computational grammar. David Marr's Vision (1982, MIT) provided the canonical framework: the brain is a computational system that can be fully described at the algorithmic level; inner experience is irrelevant to the explanation.

The funding apparatus was explicit: DARPA funded the early AI and cognitive science programs at MIT, Carnegie Mellon, and Stanford from the late 1950s as Cold War research. NSF funded the Cognitive Science Society (1979) and the journal Cognitive Science. The Sloan Foundation (1975–1985) provided $15 million specifically to establish cognitive science as an academic field, documented in its own grant records.

Why — the gain and control

DARPA's interest was military: autonomous decision-making systems, machine translation, command-and-control. Its funding assumption — that cognition is computation and the brain is a biological computer — was a research premise, not a finding. The premise became the default framework of academic psychology, linguistics, and neuroscience, reaching every undergraduate who took an introductory cognitive science course. The ontological claim delivered through this apparatus: mental life is information processing; subjective experience is either epiphenomenal (irrelevant) or identical to the computational process; there is nothing about human consciousness that exceeds its functional description. This claim was presented not as a philosophical position but as what cognitive science has established, which is the same epistemological move as logical positivism applied to mind.

Primary sources
  • Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence,' Mind, 59 (1950): primary source — the Turing Test framework.
  • David Marr, Vision: A Computational Investigation (1982): primary source — the computational framework for cognition.
  • Howard Gardner, The Mind's New Science: A History of the Cognitive Revolution (1985): documented DARPA and Sloan Foundation funding of cognitive science as a field.
  • DARPA: documented in multiple histories of early AI research — Pamela McCorduck, Machines Who Think (1979).

5142f5b43bb93046.h:
USA/Global, 1983–present

Free Will Elimination & Hard Determinism

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

Libet's NIH-funded experiments (1983), Wegner's Harvard research (2002), and Harris's mass-market books delivered 'free will is a neuroscientific illusion' to global audiences

What they did

Three distinct delivery mechanisms: Benjamin Libet (UCSF, NIH-funded) published experiments in 1983 showing that brain activity (the "readiness potential") begins ~500ms before a person reports consciously deciding to move. The interpretation — widely broadcast — was that the conscious intention is produced after the neural event, making it an epiphenomenon. Libet himself did not draw this conclusion and proposed a "veto" capacity, but the experiments were widely cited as demonstrating the illusory nature of conscious will. Daniel Wegner (Harvard, NIH-funded) published The Illusion of Conscious Will (2002) arguing that the experience of authoring our actions is a post-hoc narrative the brain constructs. Sam Harris's Free Will (2012) — 96 pages, mass market — brought the academic argument to the New Atheism audience. Translated into dozens of languages, distributed through the same network as Dawkins and Dennett.

Why — the gain and control

The ontological claim is complete and distinct: the experience of being the author of your actions — of deliberating, choosing, and being responsible — is a systematic illusion produced by your brain. This argument reaches the same population as the rest of the network's outputs and closes the last gap: if there is no soul (holbach_salon), no God (french_revolution), no objective morality (moral_nihilism), no inherent meaning (cosmic_nihilism), and no free will (free_will_elim), then what remains is a physical process running in a body in a meaningless universe — which is precisely the starting position required for the competitive-individual framework to function as the only available account of motivation. The NIH funding chain is documented in Libet's and Wegner's published acknowledgments. Harris's distribution through the New Atheism network is documented in sales figures and co-promotion records.

Primary sources
  • Benjamin Libet, 'Time of Conscious Intention to Act in Relation to Onset of Cerebral Activity,' Brain (1983): primary source — NIH funding acknowledged.
  • Daniel Wegner, The Illusion of Conscious Will (2002): primary source — Harvard/NIH funded.
  • Sam Harris, Free Will (2012): primary source — distributed through New Atheism network.
  • Alfred Mele, Free: Why Science Hasn't Disproved Free Will (2014): documented the institutional interpretation of Libet and the gap between the experiments and the conclusions drawn.
All connections
