6338e9ddfc44c680.h:
USA/EU, 2013–present

NIH BRAIN Initiative & Human Brain Project

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

NIH $500M+ and EU €1B Human Brain Project — the largest coordinated science funding in history, premised on the assumption that consciousness IS neural activity and a complete neural map will explain it

What they did

Two simultaneous initiatives announced in 2013: President Obama's BRAIN Initiative (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies) — $500 million in its first phase, ongoing — and the EU's Human Brain Project — €1 billion over 10 years (2013–2023). Their stated goal: map the complete activity of the human brain at single-neuron resolution to understand how mental function, perception, and consciousness arise from neural activity.

The premise embedded in the framing — not stated as a hypothesis but as the research question — is that consciousness and mental life are identical to or fully explained by neural activity patterns. The projects are scoped around the premise that consciousness and mental life arise from neural activity — which is not stated as a hypothesis under investigation but as the framing of every research question. The Human Brain Project scaled back its original consciousness-modeling ambitions significantly mid-project (following a 2014 open letter from 800 neuroscientists that led to a governance review) — but the underlying commitment to neural-level explanation remained the research frame throughout. Their outputs — tools, maps, datasets — are framed as progress toward understanding "the brain" as the complete explanation of "the mind," distributing that framing through every science communication, press release, and educational resource generated by the projects.

Why — the gain and control

The funding scale matters: $500M+ and €1B represent the largest single investment ever made in research premised on neuroreductionism — the claim that mental states are entirely brain states. Every tool, every dataset, every press release, and every science education resource generated by these projects carries the embedded claim that mapping the brain will explain the mind. This is not a scientific finding — it is a research premise. But presented at this scale through the most authoritative scientific institutions (NIH, EU Commission) and covered by every major science press outlet, it becomes what educated people understand science has established. The practical consequences are clinical: hospital systems globally adopted "evidence-based" psychiatric protocols premised on the biological model of mind that these projects reinforce — routing treatment toward pharmacological and neural intervention and away from relational, social, or meaning-based approaches.

Primary sources
  • NIH, BRAIN Initiative documentation (2013–present): primary source — public funding records.
  • EU Commission, Human Brain Project documentation (2013–2023): primary source — grant records.
  • Alva Noë, Out of Our Heads: Why You Are Not Your Brain (2009): documented the philosophical assumptions embedded in neuroscience's research framing — written before the initiatives but directly predictive of their assumptions.
  • Raymond Tallis, Aping Mankind: Neuromania, Darwinitis and the Misrepresentation of Humanity (2011): documented 'neuromania' as a cultural phenomenon premised on neuroreductionism.

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

What they did

Two simultaneous initiatives announced in 2013: President Obama's BRAIN Initiative (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies) — $500 million in its first phase, ongoing — and the EU's Human Brain Project — €1 billion over 10 years (2013–2023). cd43d4f320ffb396.h:
Europe, ~300–1700 CE

Papal & Church Authority

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Ran every university and library in the Western world for 1,400 years

What they did

For over a millennium the Catholic Church was the only institution in the Western world that housed books, trained scholars, and determined what knowledge was worth pursuing. Every figure who shaped early modern science — Descartes, Newton, Boyle — was educated in Church-run institutions. The Royal Society grew directly from graduates of Oxford and Cambridge, both originally Church foundations.

The Church's theological framework produced three structural conditions that made the world increasingly available for exploitation.

1. The Creator–creation gap. In classical Christian theology, God is ontologically distinct from creation — self-subsistent, uncreated, not continuous with the world. Creation is contingent: it depends on God for its existence at every moment, has no inherent self-sufficiency, and is not itself divine. This establishes a permanent metaphysical gap between ultimate reality and the material world. In most pre-Christian cosmologies — animist, Neoplatonic, Vedantic, indigenous — the world is either divine manifestation, continuous with divine emanation, or permeated by sacred presence. Harming a river or a forest was harming something that participated in ultimate reality. Under Creator–creation dualism, the world is created artifact: contingent, finite, neutral. A metaphysically neutral world is a world available to be used.

2. The subject–object structure. Because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–28), they inherit a derivative subject-position over the rest of creation. The structure is: God as absolute subject → humans as subordinate subjects → nature as object. The explicit Genesis mandate — "subdue the earth, have dominion over every living thing" — was the operative theological framework that every early modern scientist, merchant, and colonial administrator was educated within. Once nature is object rather than participant, it becomes measurable, extractable, and reconfigurable. Extraction is not desecration of the sacred. It is proper use of the created.

3. Deferred fulfillment. The present world is a temporary passage toward a post-mortem destination. Ultimate reality is not here. This structure makes present-world suffering spiritually intelligible — it is temporary — and makes resistance to material conditions a form of misplaced attachment to what is, by definition, not ultimate. When ultimate fulfillment is deferred to another existence, the present world becomes instrumentalizable in two directions simultaneously: resource to be extracted by those with power, trial to be endured by those without.

Why — the gain and control

The Church's monopoly on education was the foundation of its political and economic power — who controls what counts as knowledge controls what people believe is possible, permissible, and real.

Before the Church installed Creator–creation dualism across European and colonized populations, most human cosmologies were participatory: land, rivers, animals, and ancestors were participants in shared reality with their own standing. The Church's relationship to these frameworks was not simply eliminative — the historical record is more complex. In its early centuries, the Church competed directly with paganism and forcibly suppressed it in some regions. But through much of its medieval dominance, the relationship was more syncretic: the Church absorbed, repurposed, and Christianized local practices — saints replacing local deities, feast days mapped onto seasonal celebrations, folk healing practices tolerated under clerical supervision. The participatory cosmologies were more often transformed than destroyed. What the process eliminated was their ontological authority: a river spirit that becomes a saint is still a river spirit, but it is now a created being subordinate to a transcendent God, not a co-participant in reality with its own standing. The desacralization was structural, operating through transformation rather than always through destruction. The endpoint — a world of created objects under human stewardship — was the same.

When the Royal Society and the merchant class needed a philosophy that made the world freely exploitable, they did not need to invent it. It was already installed. Descartes, Newton, Boyle — trained by the Church — inherited a world already understood as contingent artifact rather than sacred participant. Secular science removed God from the picture but kept the structure: discrete, non-divine, non-ensouled objects available to be measured, owned, and extracted. The subject–object hierarchy remained identical. Only the authorization changed — from divine command to natural law.

Beyond the metaphysics, the Church defined what correct inner life should look like, required its disclosure, and used the gap between the person's actual desires and the approved framework to redirect them into compliance. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) made annual confession compulsory: "Every faithful of either sex shall after the attainment of years of discretion faithfully confess all their sins at least once a year to their own priest" (Canon 21). The confessor did not merely absolve — he categorized desires for material improvement as avarice, resistance to authority as pride, and acceptance of suffering as virtue.

The tithe — one-tenth of agricultural production — requires accurate framing. Canon law specified the quadripartite division: a quarter each to the bishop, the local clergy, the poor, and church maintenance. The Church had a documented obligation to provide for the poor from these revenues, and in many periods this functioned as the primary welfare system in Europe. That obligation was real, if frequently violated in practice, and presenting tithe income as pure extraction misrepresents the legal and moral framework it operated within. What remains documentable is the outcome: the Church held approximately one-third of all agricultural land in Western Europe by 1200 CE (R.W. Southern, Western Society and the Church in the Middle Ages, 1970), and the three structural conditions above — neutral matter, authorized extraction, internalized desire-suppression — prepared the ground for the secular extraction apparatus that followed.

Primary sources
  • Steven Shapin & Simon Schaffer, Leviathan and the Air-Pump (1985): documented how the Royal Society's experimental practice encoded specific authority relationships inherited from Church institutional culture.
  • Frances Yates, The Rosicrucian Enlightenment (1972): traced the esoteric and commercial networks that preceded the Royal Society's formation.

3da97616108c3a5d.h:
Europe, ~300–1700 CE

Papal & Church Authority

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1620–1780 · The World Becomes a Machine

Ran every university and library in the Western world for 1,400 years

What they did

For over a millennium the Catholic Church was the only institution in the Western world that housed books, trained scholars, and determined what knowledge was worth pursuing. Every figure who shaped early modern science — Descartes, Newton, Boyle — was educated in Church-run institutions. The Royal Society grew directly from graduates of Oxford and Cambridge, both originally Church foundations.

The Church's theological framework produced three structural conditions that made the world increasingly available for exploitation.

1. The Creator–creation gap. In classical Christian theology, God is ontologically distinct from creation — self-subsistent, uncreated, not continuous with the world. Creation is contingent: it depends on God for its existence at every moment, has no inherent self-sufficiency, and is not itself divine. This establishes a permanent metaphysical gap between ultimate reality and the material world. In most pre-Christian cosmologies — animist, Neoplatonic, Vedantic, indigenous — the world is either divine manifestation, continuous with divine emanation, or permeated by sacred presence. Harming a river or a forest was harming something that participated in ultimate reality. Under Creator–creation dualism, the world is created artifact: contingent, finite, neutral. A metaphysically neutral world is a world available to be used.

2. The subject–object structure. Because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:26–28), they inherit a derivative subject-position over the rest of creation. The structure is: God as absolute subject → humans as subordinate subjects → nature as object. The explicit Genesis mandate — "subdue the earth, have dominion over every living thing" — was the operative theological framework that every early modern scientist, merchant, and colonial administrator was educated within. Once nature is object rather than participant, it becomes measurable, extractable, and reconfigurable. Extraction is not desecration of the sacred. It is proper use of the created.

3. Deferred fulfillment. The present world is a temporary passage toward a post-mortem destination. Ultimate reality is not here. This structure makes present-world suffering spiritually intelligible — it is temporary — and makes resistance to material conditions a form of misplaced attachment to what is, by definition, not ultimate. When ultimate fulfillment is deferred to another existence, the present world becomes instrumentalizable in two directions simultaneously: resource to be extracted by those with power, trial to be endured by those without.

Why — the gain and control

The Church's monopoly on education was the foundation of its political and economic power — who controls what counts as knowledge controls what people believe is possible, permissible, and real.

Before the Church installed Creator–creation dualism across European and colonized populations, most human cosmologies were participatory: land, rivers, animals, and ancestors were participants in shared reality with their own standing. The Church's relationship to these frameworks was not simply eliminative — the historical record is more complex. In its early centuries, the Church competed directly with paganism and forcibly suppressed it in some regions. But through much of its medieval dominance, the relationship was more syncretic: the Church absorbed, repurposed, and Christianized local practices — saints replacing local deities, feast days mapped onto seasonal celebrations, folk healing practices tolerated under clerical supervision. The participatory cosmologies were more often transformed than destroyed. What the process eliminated was their ontological authority: a river spirit that becomes a saint is still a river spirit, but it is now a created being subordinate to a transcendent God, not a co-participant in reality with its own standing. The desacralization was structural, operating through transformation rather than always through destruction. The endpoint — a world of created objects under human stewardship — was the same.

When the Royal Society and the merchant class needed a philosophy that made the world freely exploitable, they did not need to invent it. It was already installed. Descartes, Newton, Boyle — trained by the Church — inherited a world already understood as contingent artifact rather than sacred participant. Secular science removed God from the picture but kept the structure: discrete, non-divine, non-ensouled objects available to be measured, owned, and extracted. The subject–object hierarchy remained identical. Only the authorization changed — from divine command to natural law.

Beyond the metaphysics, the Church defined what correct inner life should look like, required its disclosure, and used the gap between the person's actual desires and the approved framework to redirect them into compliance. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) made annual confession compulsory: "Every faithful of either sex shall after the attainment of years of discretion faithfully confess all their sins at least once a year to their own priest" (Canon 21). The confessor did not merely absolve — he categorized desires for material improvement as avarice, resistance to authority as pride, and acceptance of suffering as virtue.

That obligation was real, if frequently violated in practice, and presenting tithe income as pure extraction misrepresents the legal and moral framework it operated within. f519997a0af9dc74.h:
USA/UK, 1990–present

Analytic Metaphysics & Eliminativism

Institution · period on the page's diagram: 1970–Now · Into Every Mind

Peter van Inwagen, Peter Unger — analytic philosophers at elite universities arguing most ordinary objects and persons do not exist; funded through standard philosophy department budgets at Notre Dame, NYU, Princeton

What they did

Two distinct threads of analytic metaphysics arrived at similar eliminativist conclusions: Peter van Inwagen's Material Beings (1990, Syracuse/Notre Dame) argued that composite physical objects — tables, chairs, and human persons as ordinarily understood — do not exist. Only simples (fundamental particles) and living organisms exist. The person you take yourself to be is a physical organism, not a person in any richer sense. Peter Unger's Empty Ideas (2014, NYU) argued that most philosophical concepts, including person, self, and object, are empty — no philosophical theory about them can be true because they don't pick out anything real.

These positions were published through Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press — the most prestigious academic publishers — and are standard reference points in graduate metaphysics seminars globally. Their departmental funding was through standard philosophy faculty positions at Notre Dame (van Inwagen), NYU (Unger), and Princeton, where this style of metaphysics has been the dominant approach since the 1970s.

Why — the gain and control

The significance for this network is not that van Inwagen or Unger intended ideological effects — they understood themselves as doing rigorous philosophy. The significance is the educational output: graduate students in analytic philosophy trained at Notre Dame, NYU, and Princeton carry the eliminativist framework into the philosophy departments where undergraduates receive their one or two required philosophy courses. A framework in which the person you take yourself to be does not exist as ordinarily understood — in which "person" is either reducible to physical particles or empty of reference — completes the metaphysical dissolution that the network's earlier nodes began. Van Inwagen himself is a Christian; Unger is not ideologically motivated. The framework's consequences are independent of their intentions.

Primary sources
  • Peter van Inwagen, Material Beings (1990): primary source — Notre Dame/Syracuse; Oxford University Press.
  • Peter Unger, Empty Ideas: A Critique of Analytic Philosophy (2014): primary source — NYU; Oxford University Press.
  • Kit Fine, 'The Question of Realism,' Philosophers' Imprint (2001): documented the context of metaphysical eliminativism in analytic philosophy departments.

5891f3e939e6a9e4.h:
Athens, ~387–86 BCE

Plato & The Academy

Thinker · period on the page's diagram: 400 BCE – 1620 CE · Ancient & Medieval Roots

The world of the senses is a shadow — only abstract Forms are real; the philosopher-king should govern because he alone can perceive true reality

What they did

Plato's Republic (~380 BCE) established an institutional template that every subsequent node in this visualization replicated: a school that trains an accredited class in the correct perception of reality and credentials them to govern those who cannot perceive it. The philosopher, trained in the Academy's methods, has direct access to the Forms — the underlying principles of Justice, Truth, and the Good that ordinary perception cannot reach. This epistemological hierarchy — some people perceive real reality, most do not — became the structural blueprint for the Church's theological schools, the Royal Society's definition of empirical knowledge, the university system's credentialing apparatus, and the economic think-tank's claim to perceive how markets really work.

The Academy ran continuously for 900 years — from its founding around 387 BCE until the Emperor Justinian closed it in 529 CE — making it the longest-running institution of its kind in Western history and the direct template for the medieval university system.

Note on what Plato does not claim: Plato explicitly forbids the philosopher-king class from holding private property (Republic 416d–417b) and treats harm done in the physical world as morally serious — injustice damages the soul, which is metaphysically real. The claim sometimes made that his metaphysics licenses material exploitation is not textually supported. The connection between hierarchical epistemology and extraction is genealogical, not doctrinal.

Why — the gain and control

The expert-class template Plato institutionalized has two politically consequential features that subsequent nodes in this visualization inherited and adapted.

First: knowledge confers governing authority. If the philosopher perceives a reality inaccessible to ordinary people — whether that reality is Platonic Forms, God's will, natural law, empirical science, or economic efficiency — then the opposition of those ordinary people to governance by that expert class is not a political claim with standing. It is ignorance of what is actually real. This structure pre-empts dissent by reclassifying it as confusion rather than legitimate disagreement. The Church's theologians, the Royal Society's empiricists, the Chicago School economists, and the psychiatric classification systems all replicate this structure: each claims access to a reality (divine, physical, economic, psychological) that non-experts cannot directly perceive, and each uses that claim to define deviation from their governance as error rather than resistance.

Second: the Academy institutionalized credentialing. The claim to perceive higher reality was not merely asserted — it was certified by membership in an institution with controlled entry standards. That certification structure — who may legitimately speak about what is real — became the operational mechanism of every knowledge institution in this visualization. Membership in the Royal Society, the university, the economics department, the board-certified psychiatric establishment: each derives its authority from the Platonic template of the accredited school that certifies correct perception of reality.

The genealogical argument that transcendent metaphysics tends toward objectification of the sensory world — running from Nietzsche through Heidegger to post-structural critics — is a real and serious intellectual tradition. But it is an argument about the consequences of dualistic metaphysics built on Plato's framework by later thinkers, not Plato's stated doctrine. What is directly documentable for this visualization is the institutional template: the school that certifies reality-perception and credentials governance.

Primary sources
  • Plato, Republic (~380 BCE), especially Books VI–VII (the Allegory of the Cave and the Form of the Good): primary source.
  • Harold Cherniss, The Riddle of the Early Academy (1945): documented the Academy's institutional structure and 900-year continuity.
  • Julia Annas, An Introduction to Plato's Republic (1981): standard scholarly account of the philosopher-king and Forms.

bc2fbd89ce923ce3.h:
Global, ~800–200 BCE

Axial Age State Religion

Government · period on the page's diagram: 400 BCE – 1620 CE · Ancient & Medieval Roots

Every reform movement — Buddha, Confucius, the Hebrew prophets — was absorbed by an empire within two centuries; the axial breakthrough became imperial ideology

What they did

The philosopher Karl Jaspers identified the period ~800–200 BCE as the Axial Age — when, simultaneously across China, India, Persia, Israel, and Greece, major thinkers broke from mythological frameworks to address the human condition directly: the Buddha (~500 BCE), Confucius (~500 BCE), the Hebrew prophets (~750–550 BCE), Zoroaster (~600 BCE), Socrates and Plato (~400 BCE). Each addressed the question of how to live rightly in a world of suffering and impermanence.

Each of these movements was then absorbed by an imperial apparatus within two centuries: Buddhism became the state religion of the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka (~260 BCE); Confucianism became the state ideology of the Han Dynasty (~200 BCE); the Hebrew prophetic tradition was canonized by the Persian-sponsored return from Babylon; Platonism became the philosophical framework of the Roman imperial administration. In each case, the framework moved from a critique of power to a legitimation of power within two to three generations.

Why — the gain and control

Each framework that began as a critique of extraction was absorbed by institutional power and converted into its legitimating ideology — specifically because it resolved the problem of compliance without force.

Buddhism offers the most complex case and the one most requiring qualification. The doctrine that suffering arises from attachment — to land, community, descendants, the living world — can be read, when institutionalized by empire, as providing philosophical cover for extraction: a population that understands attachment as the source of suffering may be less likely to resist dispossession. This is a specific critical theory reading of Buddhism's political function, not a claim about what the Buddha taught or what Buddhist practitioners have understood themselves to be doing. Ashoka's actual relationship to Buddhism is contested: his edicts show concern for animal welfare, religious tolerance, and reduced violence rather than straightforward extraction legitimation. The argument here is about how Buddhist frameworks were available to be used by subsequent imperial and colonial apparatuses — British colonial administrators in Burma and Ceylon explicitly used non-attachment doctrine in this way (Philip Almond, The British Discovery of Buddhism, 1988). The function of the framework in a given political context requires case-by-case historical documentation, not a general claim about the doctrine itself.

Confucianism's emphasis on hierarchical obligation — the ruler-subject, parent-child, elder-younger bonds — was adopted by the Han Dynasty precisely because it provided a complete philosophical account of why subjects owe obedience to their rulers, making extraction through taxation and corvée labor appear as the natural expression of cosmic order rather than coercion.

Early Christianity was a movement of enslaved people, urban poor, and dispossessed provincials — its core teaching was that the powerful would be humbled and the poor exalted, that wealth was a spiritual danger. Within eighty years of Constantine's adoption of the faith, it was the only legal religion of the empire. The same doctrine of patient suffering ("blessed are the meek") that had sustained people under exploitation now became the official teaching of the institution administering the Roman tax system. The deferred-compensation structure of Christian salvation — accept poverty and suffering now; receive eternal reward later — made temporal extraction not merely bearable but spiritually correct. The serf who gave a third of her harvest to the lord and a tenth to the Church was doing what God required. Resistance was not injustice; it was sin.

The mechanism varies: Christianity's deferred compensation, Confucianism's hierarchical obligation, Buddhism's non-attachment. Each framework that began as a critique of extraction was absorbed by institutional power and converted into its legitimating ideology — specifically because it resolved the problem of compliance without force.
